before: 'And bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.' (Matthew 6:13) The 'but deliver us from evil' (Matthew 10:29) is passed over in silence with Luke. If the Savior does not command us to pray impossibilities, it seems to me worth inquiring how we are commanded to pray not to enter 'into temptation' — when the whole life of men on earth is a trial. For as long as we are on earth, girt with the flesh that wars 'against the spirit' — whose 'mind' is 'enmity' 'toward God,' wholly unable to submit 'to God's law' — we are in temptation.

That all human life 'on earth' is a 'trial,' we learned from Job in these words: 'Is not man's life on earth a trial?' The same is declared by the seventeenth Psalm in the 'In thee I shall be delivered from trial.' (Romans 8:7) And Paul, writing to the Corinthians, says God grants not freedom from being tempted but freedom from being tempted beyond power: 'No temptation has taken you but human; but God is faithful, who will not suffer you to be tempted beyond what you can, but will make with the temptation also the way out, that you may be able to bear it.' (Galatians 5:17) For whether our 'wrestling' is 'against' the lusting flesh, or the flesh warring 'against the spirit,' or against the soul 'of all flesh' — which is homonymous with the body it inhabits, the ruling faculty, called 'heart' — such is the 'wrestling' of those to be tempted with human temptations; or whether, as advanced and more perfect athletes — no longer 'wrestling against blood and flesh,' (Job 40:8 (LXX)) nor examined in the human temptations they have already trodden down — our contests are 'against the principalities and the authorities and the world-rulers of this darkness, and the spiritual hosts of wickedness' (Job 7:1) — we have not been freed from being tempted.

How, then, does the Savior command us to pray not to enter 'into temptation' — when God in a way tempts all? 'Remember,' says Judith — if not to the elders of that time only but to all who meet with her writing — 'what he did with Abraham, and what he tempted Isaac with, and what befell Jacob in Mesopotamia of Syria, feeding Laban's sheep, his mother's brother's. For not as he fired those into a proving of their heart does the Lord who scourges unto admonition those who draw near him avenge us.' And as a general saying concerning all righteous men, David says: 'Many are the afflictions of the righteous' (Psalm 17:30 (LXX)); and the Apostle in the Acts: 'Through many afflictions we must enter into God's kingdom.'

And unless we understand what escapes most concerning praying not to enter 'into temptation,' it is time to say that the apostles, praying, were not heard — suffering myriads through their whole lifetime: 'in labors more abundantly, in stripes above measure, in prisons more frequently, in deaths often' (1 Corinthians 10:13); and Paul in particular 'received from the Jews five times forty save one,' (Ephesians 6:12) 'was thrice beaten with rods,' (Deuteronomy 8:2–5,15–16) 'once stoned,' 'thrice shipwrecked,' 'spent a night and day in the deep' (Romans 8:28) — a man 'in all things' afflicted and perplexed and persecuted and cast down, confessing too that 'even unto this present hour we hunger and thirst and are naked and buffeted and homeless, and labor, working with our own hands; being reviled, we bless; being persecuted, we endure; being blasphemed, we entreat.' (Judith 8:21–27) But if the apostles, in praying, did not obtain — what hope has one inferior to them, praying, of obtaining a hearing God?

One who does not examine exactly what the Savior's commandment wills may reasonably suppose the 'Prove me, O Lord, and tempt me; fire my reins and my heart' (Psalm 33:20 (LXX)) in the twenty-fifth Psalm to be contrary to what our Lord taught concerning prayer. But when did anyone deem a man to be outside temptations — whose word he knew fulfilled? And what season is there in which, as not wrestling over not sinning, he has despised caution? Is one poor? Let him beware, lest stealing he swear 'by God's name.' Is one rich? Let him not despise caution: for, filled, he can become 'false,' and, lifted up, say 'Who sees me?' Not even Paul, rich 'in all speech and all knowledge,' (Song of Songs 2:9–10) was freed from the danger of sinning in self-exaltation over these — he needs 'a thorn of Satan buffeting' (Job 40:8) him, 'lest' he 'be exalted.' And if one is conscious of better things and is winged away from evils, let him read what is said in Second Chronicles concerning Hezekiah — who is said to have fallen 'from the height of his heart.'

And if one despises caution because we said no more of the poor man — as though there were no temptation concerning poverty — let him know that the plotter plots 'to cast down the poor and needy' — especially since, according to Solomon, 'the poor abides not threat.' And why speak of how many, through bodily wealth, ill-stewarded, received in punishment the place with the rich man in the Gospel? And how many, basely bearing poverty — conducting themselves more slavishly and lowly than befits 'the saints' — fell from the heavenly hope? Nor are those between the two — on either side, wealth and poverty, in measured possession — altogether freed from sinning.

But one healthy and vigorous in body supposes, in the very being healthy and vigorous, that he is outside all temptation. And whose sin is it, but the healthy and vigorous, 'to destroy the temple of God' — which no one will dare speak plainly of in detail, since what concerns that place lies openly before all? And what sick man escapes the provocations to 'destroy God's temple' — leisured at that season, readily receiving thoughts of impure matters? And what disturbs him beyond these — unless 'with all guard' he keep his 'heart' — why even speak? For many, overcome by pains and unable to bear diseases manfully, were then proved sick in soul rather than in bodies. And many, fleeing disgrace — ashamed to bear Christ's noble name nobly — fell into eternal shame.

But one supposes he rests, as not tempted, when glorified among men. And how is the 'they have received their reward,' announced 'from men' to those elated by glory among the many for good, not grievous? And how is the 'How can you believe, receiving glory from one another, and seeking not the glory that comes from the only God?' (Acts 14:22) not rebuking? And why must I recount the falls in pride of the deemed well-born, and of the deemed low-born the untaught fawning suspicion toward those deemed to excel — which draws men from God: who have no genuine friendship, but play the hypocrite toward the fairest of things among men — love?

All 'life,' then, as aforesaid, of 'man upon earth' 'is' a trial. That is why we pray to be delivered from trial — not in not being tempted (for that is impossible, especially for those 'on earth'), but in not being defeated when tempted. I take the defeated in temptation to enter 'into' temptation, held in its nets. Into these nets, for the sake of those already caught in them, the Savior entered — 'stooping through the nets,' as said in the Song of Songs — and 'answers' those already caught by them, who entered 'into' temptation, and says, as 'bride' to his 'bride': 'Rise, come, my neighbor, my fair one, my dove.' (2 Corinthians 11:23–27) And I shall add, to persuade that every season is a season of temptation for men: not even 'he who meditates God's law day and night,' who strives to accomplish the 'mouth of the righteous shall meditate wisdom,' (1 Corinthians 4:11–13) is freed from being tempted.

At any rate, those who, declining in devoting themselves to the examination of divine Scriptures, devoted themselves to godless and impious doctrines — or to silly and laughable ones — why speak of them? When myriads who seem not liable to the charge of neglecting the readings trip over such things? The same befalls many with the apostolic and evangelical readings too — who through their own folly fashion another Son or Father beside the one theologized and truly known to the saints. For he who thinks untrue things concerning God or his Christ has fallen from the true God and his Only-begotten; and the one his folly fashioned, supposing it Father and Son, he does not truly worship — suffering this because he did not perceive the temptation in reading holy things, nor armed himself and stood against the contest then present to him also.

We must pray, then, not that we be not tempted (for that is impossible), but that we be not encompassed by temptation — which those held in it and overcome suffer. Since, then, outside the prayer it is written 'not to enter into temptation' — which, from what is said, can somehow be plain — and in the prayer we must say to God the Father 'bring us not into temptation' — it is worth seeing how we must conceive God bringing into temptation the one who did not pray, or the one not heard. For it sounds ill to conceive God bringing anyone 'into temptation' — with the overcome entering 'into' temptation — as though, by his being overcome, God handed him over. And the same ill sound awaits one who in any way expounds the 'pray not to enter into temptation.' For if falling 'into temptation' is evil — against suffering which we pray — how is it not absurd to conceive the good God, who cannot 'bear evil fruits,' encompassing anyone with evils?

Useful for this, then, is to set beside it what Paul said in Romans, in this way: 'Professing to be wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and quadrupeds and creeping things. Therefore God handed them over, in the lusts of their hearts, unto uncleanness, to dishonor their bodies among themselves.' (Psalm 25:2) And after a little: 'For this God handed them over to passions of dishonor' (Proverbs 30:9); and 'handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting.' (2 Corinthians 12:7) Were those not handed over to them by God not made 'in the lusts of their own hearts'? Would those not handed over by God to 'passions of dishonor' have fallen under them? Would they have collapsed 'into a reprobate mind' without being handed to it by God — those so condemned?

Those, then — I well know these things will greatly trouble them, and that is why they fashion another god beside the maker of heaven and earth, since, finding many such things in the Law and the Prophets, they stumbled at them, as at one not good who utters such voices. But for us — with the difficulties already raised concerning the 'bring us not into temptation,' for which we set out the apostolic words too — we must see whether we also find worthy loosenings of the ill sounds. I take God to dispense each rational soul with an eye to its eternal life — which ever keeps its self-determination — and, by its own cause, either among the better, ascending to the summit of goods, or descending variously, through inattention, into such-and-such a bilge of evil. Since, then, speedy healing, and more compendious, breeds in some a contempt of the diseases into which they fell — easily healed, so that after healing they would fall a second time into the same — reasonably, in such cases, he overlooks wickedness growing for a time, and, spreading longer in them, overlooks it as incurable: that, by spending time with evil and being glutted with the sin they desire, they may be sated, perceive the harm, hate what they formerly welcomed, and, healed, be able more firmly to profit from the health belonging to being healed in their souls. As the 'mixed multitude' 'among the sons of Israel 'lusted a lust, and, sitting down, the sons of Israel wept too, and said: Who shall feed us flesh? We remembered the fish we ate freely in Egypt, and the cucumbers and the melons and the leeks and the onions and the garlic. But now our soul is dry; nothing but the manna are our eyes.' (2 Chronicles 32:25–26) Then after a little it is said: 'And Moses heard them weeping by their families, each at his door.' (Proverbs 13:8) And again after a little the Lord says to Moses: 'And to the people thou shalt say: Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat flesh — for you wept before the Lord, saying: Who shall feed us flesh? For it was well with us in Egypt. And the Lord shall give you flesh to eat, and you shall eat flesh. Not one day shall you eat, nor two, nor five days, nor ten days, nor twenty days — unto a month of days shall you eat, until it come out of your nostrils, and be cholera to you — because you disobeyed the Lord, who is among you, and wept before him, saying: Why did we come out of Egypt?' (1 Corinthians 3:17)

Let us see, then, whether we usefully compared this history toward loosing the ill sound in the 'bring us not into temptation' and in the apostolic words. Lusting 'a lust,' 'the mixed multitude' among the sons of Israel — Israel wept with them. And it is plain that, without what they lusted for, they could take no fill of them, nor cease from the passion. But the philanthropic and good God, giving them what they lusted for, did not so will to give as to leave lust remaining in them. That is why he says they shall eat the 'flesh' not 'one day' — for their passion would have remained in their soul, fired and kindled by it, if they had shared flesh for a little — nor 'two' days does he give them what they lusted for. Wishing to make it loathsome to them, he as it were promises not, but threatens the discerning through what he seemed to grant — saying: you shall not make 'five' days 'only' eating the 'flesh,' nor twice those, nor yet twice those — but 'you shall eat' so long, feasting on flesh a whole month, 'until it come out of your nostrils,' (Proverbs 4:23) with choleric suffering, the deemed good and the blameworthy, shameful lust for it. That I may free you from life no longer lusting — and, so delivered, you may, as pure from lust, and remembering from how many pains you were freed of it, either never fall into it again, or — if ever this happens — after long circuits of years, forgetting what you suffered through lust — unless you attend to yourselves and take up the Word that wholly frees from all passion — fall into evils afterwards, and, lusting after procreation(?), beg to obtain twice what you lust for, hating the lusted, and then so run back to the good and the heavenly food, which, despising, they reached for the worse.

The like, then, shall those suffer who 'changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and quadrupeds and creeping things' (Matthew 6:2) — by being forsaken, handed 'in the lusts of their hearts unto uncleanness, to dishonor the bodies' (John 5:44) of those who degraded the name of him who grants to all sentient rationals not only sensing, but to some sensing rationally, and to some perfectly and virtuously sensing and understanding. And reasonably such are handed over by the God forsaken by them — forsaken in turn by him — to 'passions of dishonor,' receiving 'the recompense' 'of the error' they loved, 'wasting(?)' 'pleasure.' For the 'recompense of error' comes upon them, handed 'to passions of dishonor,' rather than upon those cleansed by wise fire. And in prison they are exacted to the last quadrans for each of their debts. For in being handed to 'dishonoring' passions — not only the natural but many unnatural — they are polluted and thickened by flesh, as though having then neither soul nor mind, but becoming wholly fleshes. But in fire and prison, receiving not 'recompense of error' but benefaction unto cleansing of the evils in error, with saving pains following the pleasure-loving, they are freed from all pitch and blood — in which, befouled and bemired, they could not even conceive of being saved, by their own destruction. 'God shall wash,' then, 'the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and cleanse the blood from their midst, by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.' (Song of Songs 2:9–10,13) For 'he comes as a refiner's fire and as fullers' herb,' washing and cleansing those in need of such drugs, because they would not approvedly 'hold God in knowledge.' Handed to these, they shall willingly hate the 'reprobate mind.' For God wills the good to come to no one as by necessity, but willingly — though some, from longer commerce with evil, hardly perceive its shame, and turn from it as falsely supposed good.

But consider whether for this too God hardens Pharaoh's heart: that what he said unhardened he may be able to say — 'The Lord is righteous; I and my people are wicked.' (Psalm 1:2) Yet one needs to be hardened further and suffer further — lest, from ceasing to be hardened too quickly, despising hardening as evil, he become again more often worthy of being hardened. If, then, 'nets are not unrighteously spread for the winged,' (Romans 1:22–28) according to Proverbs, but God reasonably 'brings into the snare' — according to him who said, 'Thou broughtest us into the snare' — and 'without' the Father's 'will' not even the cheapest of winged sparrows falls 'into the snare' (falling 'into the snare' for this reason: that he used ill the wings given for rising, by his authority) — let us pray to do nothing worthy of being brought 'into' 'temptation' by God's righteous judgment: with everyone handed by God 'in the lusts' of his own heart 'unto uncleanness' being brought in, and everyone handed 'to passions of dishonor,' and everyone, 'as he approved not holding God' in himself, handed 'to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting.' (Isaiah 4:4)

The need of being tempted is something like this. What our soul received — hidden from all but God, and even from ourselves — becomes manifest through temptations: that we no longer be hidden from ourselves, whatever we are, but, knowing even ourselves, perceive, if we will, our own evils, and give thanks for the goods manifested to us through temptations. That temptations come to manifest us, whatever we are, or to discern what is hidden in our heart, is shown by what the Lord said to Job, and what stands written in Deuteronomy, running thus: 'Thinkest thou that I dealt with thee otherwise than that thou mightest appear righteous?' (Malachi 3:2) And in Deuteronomy thus: 'He afflicted thee and starved thee and fed thee manna' (Exodus 9:27) — and led thee 'in the wilderness,' 'where biting serpent and scorpion and thirst' (Proverbs 1:17) — 'that' 'what is in thy heart be discerned.'

And if we wish to be reminded from history too, know that Eve's easy-deceivability and the rottenness of her reasoning did not begin when, disobeying God, she heard the serpent — it was convicted even before, with the serpent approaching her for this reason: that in his own prudence he laid hold of her weakness. Nor did wickedness begin to come to be in Cain when he 'killed' his 'brother' — for even before, 'upon Cain and his sacrifices he had no regard' (Psalm 66:11 (LXX)) — O heart-knowing God! — but his wickedness came to light when he ... Abel. Nor, unless Noah, drinking 'of the wine' he farmed, 'was drunken' and 'was uncovered,' would either Ham's precipitance and impiety toward his father have appeared, or his brothers' reverence and shame toward their begetter. And Esau's plot against Jacob seemed to take as pretext the 'blessing's' removal — but even before this his soul held roots of being 'profane' and 'unholy.' And Joseph's chastity-brightness — prepared not to be caught by any lust — we would not have known, had his mistress not loved him.

That is why, standing in the intervals between successions of temptations, toward what is present, we are prepared for all that can befall — that, whatever happens, we be not convicted as unready, but manifest as having most diligently knit ourselves together. For what falls short through human weakness — when we accomplish all things in ourselves — God shall fulfill: who 'works all things together for good' 'to those who love' him, 'to those foreseen' by his unlying foreknowledge, whatever they shall be with him.

Useful for this, then, is to set beside it what Paul said in Romans, in this way: 'Professing to be wise, they became fools, and changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and quadrupeds and creeping things. Therefore God handed them over, in the lusts of their hearts, unto uncleanness, to dishonor their bodies among themselves.' (Romans 1:22-24) And after a little: 'For this God handed them over to passions of dishonor' (Romans 1:26); and 'handed them over to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting.' (Romans 1:28) Were those not handed over to them by God not made 'in the lusts of their own hearts'? Would those not handed over by God to 'passions of dishonor' have fallen under them? Would they have collapsed 'into a reprobate mind' without being handed to it by God — those so condemned?

Those, then — I well know these things will greatly trouble them, and that is why they fashion another god beside the maker of heaven and earth, since, finding many such things in the Law and the Prophets, they stumbled at them, as at one not good who utters such voices. But for us — with the difficulties already raised concerning the 'bring us not into temptation,' for which we set out the apostolic words too — we must see whether we also find worthy loosenings of the ill sounds. I take God to dispense each rational soul with an eye to its eternal life — which ever keeps its self-determination — and, by its own cause, either among the better, ascending to the summit of goods, or descending variously, through inattention, into such-and-such a bilge of evil. Since, then, speedy healing, and more compendious, breeds in some a contempt of the diseases into which they fell — easily healed, so that after healing they would fall a second time into the same — reasonably, in such cases, he overlooks wickedness growing for a time, and, spreading longer in them, overlooks it as incurable: that, by spending time with evil and being glutted with the sin they desire, they may be sated, perceive the harm, hate what they formerly welcomed, and, healed, be able more firmly to profit from the health belonging to being healed in their souls. As the 'mixed multitude' 'among the sons of Israel 'lusted a lust, and, sitting down, the sons of Israel wept too, and said: Who shall feed us flesh? (Numbers 11:10) And again after a little the Lord says to Moses: 'And to the people thou shalt say: Sanctify yourselves for tomorrow, and you shall eat flesh — for you wept before the Lord, saying: Who shall feed us flesh? For it was well with us in Egypt. And the Lord shall give you flesh to eat, and you shall eat flesh. Not one day shall you eat, nor two, nor five days, nor ten days, nor twenty days — unto a month of days shall you eat, until it come out of your nostrils, and be cholera to you — because you disobeyed the Lord, who is among you, and wept before him, saying: Why did we come out of Egypt?' (Numbers 11:18-20)

Let us see, then, whether we usefully compared this history toward loosing the ill sound in the 'bring us not into temptation' and in the apostolic words. Lusting 'a lust,' 'the mixed multitude' among the sons of Israel — Israel wept with them. And it is plain that, without what they lusted for, they could take no fill of them, nor cease from the passion. But the philanthropic and good God, giving them what they lusted for, did not so will to give as to leave lust remaining in them. That is why he says they shall eat the 'flesh' not 'one day' — for their passion would have remained in their soul, fired and kindled by it, if they had shared flesh for a little — nor 'two' days does he give them what they lusted for. Wishing to make it loathsome to them, he as it were promises not, but threatens the discerning through what he seemed to grant — saying: you shall not make 'five' days 'only' eating the 'flesh,' nor twice those, nor yet twice those — but 'you shall eat' so long, feasting on flesh a whole month, 'until it come out of your nostrils,' (Numbers 11:20) with choleric suffering, the deemed good and the blameworthy, shameful lust for it. That I may free you from life no longer lusting — and, so delivered, you may, as pure from lust, and remembering from how many pains you were freed of it, either never fall into it again, or — if ever this happens — after long circuits of years, forgetting what you suffered through lust — unless you attend to yourselves and take up the Word that wholly frees from all passion — fall into evils afterwards, and, lusting after procreation(?), beg to obtain twice what you lust for, hating the lusted, and then so run back to the good and the heavenly food, which, despising, they reached for the worse.

The like, then, shall those suffer who 'changed the glory of the incorruptible God into the likeness of an image of corruptible man, and of birds and quadrupeds and creeping things' (Romans 1:23) — by being forsaken, handed 'in the lusts of their hearts unto uncleanness, to dishonor the bodies' (Romans 1:24) of those who degraded the name of him who grants to all sentient rationals not only sensing, but to some sensing rationally, and to some perfectly and virtuously sensing and understanding. And reasonably such are handed over by the God forsaken by them — forsaken in turn by him — to 'passions of dishonor,' receiving 'the recompense' 'of the error' they loved, 'wasting(?)' 'pleasure.' For the 'recompense of error' comes upon them, handed 'to passions of dishonor,' rather than upon those cleansed by wise fire. And in prison they are exacted to the last quadrans for each of their debts. For in being handed to 'dishonoring' passions — not only the natural but many unnatural — they are polluted and thickened by flesh, as though having then neither soul nor mind, but becoming wholly fleshes. But in fire and prison, receiving not 'recompense of error' but benefaction unto cleansing of the evils in error, with saving pains following the pleasure-loving, they are freed from all pitch and blood — in which, befouled and bemired, they could not even conceive of being saved, by their own destruction. 'God shall wash,' then, 'the filth of the sons and daughters of Zion, and cleanse the blood from their midst, by a spirit of judgment and a spirit of burning.' (Isaiah 4:4) For 'he comes as a refiner's fire and as fullers' herb,' washing and cleansing those in need of such drugs, because they would not approvedly 'hold God in knowledge.' Handed to these, they shall willingly hate the 'reprobate mind.' For God wills the good to come to no one as by necessity, but willingly — though some, from longer commerce with evil, hardly perceive its shame, and turn from it as falsely supposed good.

But consider whether for this too God hardens Pharaoh's heart: that what he said unhardened he may be able to say — 'The Lord is righteous; I and my people are wicked.' (Exodus 9:27) Yet one needs to be hardened further and suffer further — lest, from ceasing to be hardened too quickly, despising hardening as evil, he become again more often worthy of being hardened. If, then, 'nets are not unrighteously spread for the winged,' (Proverbs 1:17) according to Proverbs, but God reasonably 'brings into the snare' — according to him who said, 'Thou broughtest us into the snare' — and 'without' the Father's 'will' not even the cheapest of winged sparrows falls 'into the snare' (falling 'into the snare' for this reason: that he used ill the wings given for rising, by his authority) — let us pray to do nothing worthy of being brought 'into' 'temptation' by God's righteous judgment: with everyone handed by God 'in the lusts' of his own heart 'unto uncleanness' being brought in, and everyone handed 'to passions of dishonor,' and everyone, 'as he approved not holding God' in himself, handed 'to a reprobate mind, to do what is unfitting.' (Isaiah 4:4)

The need of being tempted is something like this. What our soul received — hidden from all but God, and even from ourselves — becomes manifest through temptations: that we no longer be hidden from ourselves, whatever we are, but, knowing even ourselves, perceive, if we will, our own evils, and give thanks for the goods manifested to us through temptations. That temptations come to manifest us, whatever we are, or to discern what is hidden in our heart, is shown by what the Lord said to Job, and what stands written in Deuteronomy, running thus: 'Thinkest thou that I dealt with thee otherwise than that thou mightest appear righteous?' (Job 40:8) And in Deuteronomy thus: 'He afflicted thee and starved thee and fed thee manna' (Deuteronomy 8:3) — and led thee 'in the wilderness,' 'where biting serpent and scorpion and thirst' (Deuteronomy 8:15) — 'that' 'what is in thy heart be discerned.'

And if we wish to be reminded from history too, know that Eve's easy-deceivability and the rottenness of her reasoning did not begin when, disobeying God, she heard the serpent — it was convicted even before, with the serpent approaching her for this reason: that in his own prudence he laid hold of her weakness. Nor did wickedness begin to come to be in Cain when he 'killed' his 'brother' — for even before, 'upon Cain and his sacrifices he had no regard' (Psalm 66:11 (LXX)) — O heart-knowing God! — but his wickedness came to light when he ... Abel. Nor, unless Noah, drinking 'of the wine' he farmed, 'was drunken' and 'was uncovered,' would either Ham's precipitance and impiety toward his father have appeared, or his brothers' reverence and shame toward their begetter. And Esau's plot against Jacob seemed to take as pretext the 'blessing's' removal — but even before this his soul held roots of being 'profane' and 'unholy.' And Joseph's chastity-brightness — prepared not to be caught by any lust — we would not have known, had his mistress not loved him.

That is why, standing in the intervals between successions of temptations, toward what is present, we are prepared for all that can befall — that, whatever happens, we be not convicted as unready, but manifest as having most diligently knit ourselves together. For what falls short through human weakness — when we accomplish all things in ourselves — God shall fulfill: who 'works all things together for good' 'to those who love' him, 'to those foreseen' by his unlying foreknowledge, whatever they shall be with him.

With this Word, those who believe work 'the works of God' — which are food abiding unto eternal life. And 'my Father,' he says, 'gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.' And what is more nourishing to the soul than the Word? What more precious to the mind that holds her than God's wisdom? What more fitting to the rational nature than truth?

But if someone objects to this, saying he would not teach us to ask for the daily bread as for another bread distinct from himself, let him hear that in John too, in one place he discourses of it as of another beside himself, in another as being himself the bread: as of another, in these words — 'Moses gave you not the bread from heaven,' (John 6:32) 'not the true,' 'but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven'; as of himself, he says to those who said to him, 'Evermore give us this bread': 'I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst.' And the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.' (John 6:51)

And since every food is called bread according to Scripture — as plain from its being recorded of Moses that 'bread he did not eat for forty days, and water he did not drink' (Exodus 19:5) — and varied and diverse is the nourishing Word, since not all can be nourished, by firmness and vigor, on the divine lessons — therefore, wishing to present athletic food suited to the more perfect, he says: 'The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.' He who chews my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him at the last day. For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. And I take what is said with Solomon in the Proverbs to teach that he who, through simplicity, cannot hold the more vigorous and greater doctrines — yet does not think amiss — is better than the readier, sharper man who charges more greatly upon realities but does not make plain the word of the peace and harmony of all. The wording runs thus: 'Better a portion of herbs with friendship and grace than a calf from the stall with hatred.' (Proverbs 15:17) Often, at any rate, we have welcomed a private and simpler feast with a good conscience — entertained by those who could set nothing more before us — rather than loftiness of words raised 'against the knowledge of God,' proclaiming with great plausibility a doctrine foreign to the Father who gave 'the law and the prophets,' the Father of our Lord Jesus. That our soul, then, may not sicken for lack of foods, nor die to God 'by famine of the Lord's word,' let us ask of the Father the living bread — who is the same as the daily — persuaded by our teacher and Savior, believing and living more rightly.

But what the 'daily' is must now be considered. And first know this: that the word 'daily' (epiousios) has been named by no Greek, neither of the wise nor in common private usage — but seems coined by the evangelists. At any rate Matthew and Luke agreed upon it, bringing it forth nowise differing. The translators of the Hebrew did the like in other cases too. For what Greek ever used the appellation 'give ear' (enotizou), or the 'be eared' (akoutistheti) for 'receive with ears and make hearing'? Like the appellation 'daily' (epeousion) is what stands written with Moses, spoken by God: 'But you shall be to me' 'a peculiar people' (periousios). And each word seems to me made from 'substance' (ousia) — the one declaring the bread that contributes toward substance, the other signifying the people concerned with substance and sharing in it.

Now 'substance,' properly, is conceived by those who say the subsistence of the incorporeal is prior: after the incorporeal — things stably having being, admitting neither addition nor suffering subtraction (for this is peculiar to bodies, about which increase and wasting occur, since they are fluent, needing the incoming sustainer that nourishes; if more comes in seasonally than flows away, increase occurs; if less, decrease; and perhaps some receive the incoming thing not at all, in unmixed, if I may so speak ... ). But by those who deem substance consequent, with bodies prior, its definitions are these: substance is either the first matter of beings, and that from which beings come; or the matter of bodies, and that from which bodies come; or of named things, and that from which named things come; or the first substrate without quality; or what pre-subsists for beings; or what receives all changes and alterations, itself unaltered in its own ratio; or what abides through all alteration and change. On their view substance is both qualityless and unfigured in its own ratio — having no appointed magnitude either — but is set under every quality like a ready place. And 'qualities' they ordinarily call activities and makings — wherein happenings and relations turn out to be; for they say substance shares in none of these in its own ratio, but is ever inseparable from one of them by affection — no less receptive of all the maker's activities, as he makes and changes. For the tone connate with it, pervading through all of every quality, is the cause of the economies about it. Through wholes, then, they call it changeable and through wholes divisible, and say all substance can be mingled with all — united, however.

But since, inquiring concerning substance on account of the 'daily bread' and the peculiar people, we said these things to discern what substance signifies — and bread in what went before was intelligible, which we had to ask — substance akin to the bread must necessarily be conceived: that as bodily bread, dispensed, passes into the body of the nourished and into its substance, so the 'living' bread, 'come down from heaven,' dispensed into mind and soul, may share its own power with the one who offered himself to nourishment from it. And so shall be what we ask: 'daily bread.' And again: as, according to the 'quality' of the 'food' — whether 'solid' and suited to athletes, or milky and herby — the nourished comes to be in diverse power, so it follows that, as God's Word is becomingly given — whether as milk to babes, or as herbs to the sick in season, or as flesh to contenders in season — each of the nourished, by the analogy of the Word to which he offered himself, can do this or that, and become this or that. Yet there is a deemed food that is poisonous, and another that makes sick, and another that cannot even be dispensed — all of which must by analogy be transferred to the diversities of deemed nourishing lessons. Daily bread, then, is what is most fitting to the rational nature and most akin to substance itself — procuring at once health and good habit and strength for the soul, and sharing its own immortality (for God's Word is immortal) with the one who eats it.

This daily bread, then, seems to me called by another name in Scripture 'the tree of life' — toward which he who stretches 'his hand' and takes from it 'shall live forever.' Such is the 'bread of angels man ate.' For let our mind not be so poor as to suppose the angels, who ever partake, are nourished by some bodily bread — the storied bread that came down from heaven upon those who left Egypt — with the Hebrews sharing this same bread with the angels, God's ministering spirits.

It is not untimely, as we seek the 'daily bread' and the 'tree of life' and God's wisdom — the common food of holy men and angels — to attend also to the three men recorded in Genesis, brought down with Abraham and partaking of three measures of 'fine flour' kneaded into loaves: lest these things be said barely tropically, since the saints can at times share intelligible and rational food not only with men but even with diviner powers — whether for their benefit or to display what most nourishing things they have been able to procure for themselves — with the angels rejoicing and nourished in such display, and becoming readier to co-work in every way and to breathe together thereafter toward the grasp of more and greater things, upon the nourishing lessons furnished beforehand to the rest — he having gladdened and, if I may so speak, nursed them. It is no wonder if a man nourishes angels — when even Christ confesses he stands at the 'door' and knocks, that, entering with the one who opened to him, he may sup 'with him' from that one's goods, and afterwards himself share his own with the one who first feasted the Son of God, according to his own power.

But someone will say the 'daily' (epiousion) is formed from 'coming upon' (epienai) — so that we are commanded to ask the bread proper to the coming age, which God, taking beforehand, may already grant us: so that what is, as it were, to be given tomorrow be given us 'today' — 'today' taken of the present age, 'tomorrow' of the coming. But since the former interpretation is better, so far as I am judge, let us examine what lies beside it: the 'today' with Matthew, or the 'day by day' written with Luke. It is the custom in many places of Scripture to call the whole age 'today' — as 'this is the father of the Moabites unto this day,' (Hebrews 9:26) and 'this is the father of the Ammonites unto this day,' (Ephesians 2:7) and 'this saying was spread abroad among the Jews unto this day,' (Ephesians 3:20) and in the Psalms, 'Today, if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts.' And it is no wonder that to God the whole age has the ratio of one day with us — I suppose, of even less.

And it must be examined whether the words of the feasts recorded by 'days' or 'months' or 'seasons' or 'years' or 'assemblies' refer to ages. For if 'the law has a shadow of the coming things,' the many sabbaths must be a 'shadow' of many days, and the new moons, occurring through temporal intervals — I know not with what moon attending what sun they are performed. And if the first 'month,' and the tenth day 'unto the fourteenth,' and the feast of unleavened from the fourteenth 'unto the twenty-first,' contain a 'shadow of coming things' — 'who is wise, and' to such degree a 'friend' of God, as to see, of more months, the first, and its tenth day, and what follows? And what need to speak of the feast of seven weeks of days, and of the seventh month — whose new moon is a day 'of trumpets,' and whose tenth day is a day 'of atonement' — known to the God alone who legislated them? And who has so held the mind of Christ as to grasp the seventh years of the Hebrew slaves' freedom, and the 'release' of debts, and rest from tilling the holy land? And there is one higher than the feast through seven years, called Jubilee — which, even to imagine in part, or to grasp plainly that its laws shall be fulfilled as true, belongs to none except the one who contemplated the Father's counsel concerning the ordinance in all the ages, according to his 'unsearchable' 'judgments' and his untraceable ways.

Often it came upon me to wonder, comparing two apostolic sayings, how it is the 'consummation of the ages,' at which Jesus 'has been manifested for the annulling of sins' — if ages are to come after this one. The sayings run thus: in Hebrews, 'But now once, at the consummation of the ages, he has been manifested, for the annulling of sins through his sacrifice'; in Ephesians, 'that in the coming ages he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us.' (Ephesians 2:7) Pondering such greatness, I suppose that, as the last month is the consummation of the year — after which another month's beginning sets in — so perhaps, with many ages completing, as it were, a year of ages, the present age is the consummation, after which certain coming ages shall set in, whose beginning is the coming age — and in those coming ages God shall display the riches 'of his grace in kindness' — with the most sinful, even the blasphemer against the Holy Spirit, held fast by sin in the whole present age, and from the beginning to the end, to be dispensed in the coming age afterward — how, I know not.

He, then, who saw these things, and conceived in mind a week of ages — to contemplate a holy sabbatism — and a month of ages — to see God's holy new moon — and a year of ages — to understand together the year's feasts, when every 'male' must appear 'before the Lord God' — and the proportionate years of such ages — to grasp the holy seventh year — and seven sevens of ages — to hymn the so-great Lawgiver — having examined how he can fuss over the least portion of an hour of the day of so great an age, will do everything, that, made worthy by preparation here of obtaining the daily bread, he may receive it on the 'today' day — with the 'day by day' already becoming plain from what went before. For to the God who is from boundless to boundless, the one who prays concerning not only the 'today' but in a way the 'today' of the 'day by day' — from what he can contemplate — 'beyond all measure above what we ask or conceive' — shall be able to receive, if I may speak so hyperbolically, even 'what eye saw not' and 'what ear heard not' and 'what went not up upon man's heart.'

And these things too seem to me most necessary to examine, that both the 'today' be understood and the 'day by day,' when we pray that the 'daily bread' 'be given us' from his Father. But if in the last book we shall first examine the 'our' — since it is said not 'Give us this day our daily bread' but 'Our daily bread give us day by day' — yet we must examine how this bread is 'ours.' The Apostle teaches that 'whether life or death, or things present or things to come — all' are the saints'. Concerning which there is no need to speak at present.
after: 'Give us this day our daily bread' — or as Luke has it, 'Our daily bread give us day by day.' (Matthew 6:11) Since some suppose these words are said concerning bodily food — that we pray for it — it is worth removing their false opinion by these arguments and setting forth the truth concerning the daily bread. We must say to them: how could he who says we must ask heavenly and great things — when neither is the bread dispensed into our flesh heavenly, nor is the request concerning it a great petition — as it were forgetting what he taught, command the address of an entreaty to the Father concerning an earthly and small thing?

But we, following him as teacher, shall set forth at greater length the teachings concerning this bread. He says in John, to those who came to Capernaum seeking him: 'Amen, amen, I say to you: you seek me not because you saw signs, but because you ate of the loaves and were filled.' (John 6:26–58) For he who ate 'of' the loaves blessed by Jesus and was filled with them rather seeks to grasp the Son of God more exactly, and hastens to him. That is why he well commands, saying: 'Labor not for the food that perishes, but for the food that abides unto eternal life, which the Son of Man shall give you.' (John 6:27) And when his hearers asked and said, 'What shall we do, that we may work the works of God?' (John 6:28) Jesus answered and said to them: 'This is the work of God: that you believe in him whom he sent.' (John 6:29) And God sent 'his Word and healed them,' as written in the Psalms — plainly, those who were sick. With this Word, those who believe work 'the works of God' — which are food abiding unto eternal life. And 'my Father,' he says, 'gives you the true bread from heaven. For the bread of God is he who comes down from heaven and gives life to the world.' (John 6:33) And true bread nourishes the 'true' 'man' — made 'after the image of God' — who, nourished, becomes 'after the likeness' 'of him who created.' And what is more nourishing to the soul than the Word? What more precious to the mind that holds her than God's wisdom? What more fitting to the rational nature than truth?

But if someone objects to this, saying he would not teach us to ask for the daily bread as for another bread distinct from himself, let him hear that in John too, in one place he discourses of it as of another beside himself, in another as being himself the bread: as of another, in these words — 'Moses gave you not the bread from heaven,' (John 6:32) 'not the true,' 'but my Father gives you the true bread from heaven'; as of himself, he says to those who said to him, 'Evermore give us this bread': 'I am the bread of life; he who comes to me shall not hunger, and he who believes in me shall never thirst.' (John 6:35) And after a little: 'I am the (living) bread that came down from heaven. If anyone eat of this bread, he shall live forever. And the bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.' (John 6:51)

And since every food is called bread according to Scripture — as plain from its being recorded of Moses that 'bread he did not eat for forty days, and water he did not drink' (Exodus 34:28) — and varied and diverse is the nourishing Word, since not all can be nourished, by firmness and vigor, on the divine lessons — therefore, wishing to present athletic food suited to the more perfect, he says: 'The bread that I will give is my flesh, which I will give for the life of the world.' (John 6:51) And after a little: 'Unless you eat the flesh of the Son of Man and drink his blood, you have no life in you. He who chews my flesh and drinks my blood has eternal life, and I will raise him at the last day. For my flesh is true food, and my blood is true drink. He who chews my flesh and drinks my blood abides in me, and I in him. As the living Father sent me, I too live by the Father; and he who chews me, he too shall live by me.' (John 6:53-57) And this is the 'true' 'food' — the 'flesh' of Christ, which, being 'Word,' became 'flesh,' according to the saying 'And the Word became flesh.' And when we chew and drink him, he 'tabernacled in us'; and when he is dispensed, 'we beheld his glory' is fulfilled. 'This is the bread that came down from heaven — not as the fathers ate and died; he who chews this bread shall live forever.' (John 6:58)

But Paul, discoursing to 'babes' and Corinthians walking 'after man,' says: 'Milk I gave you to drink, not food; for you were not yet able. But neither even now are you able; for you are still carnal.' (1 Corinthians 3:2) And in Hebrews: 'And you have come to need milk, not solid food. For everyone who shares milk is without experience of the word of righteousness — for he is a babe. But solid food is for the perfect, who by habit have their senses trained to discern good and evil.' (Hebrews 5:14) And I take even the 'One believes he may eat all things, but the weak eats herbs' (Romans 14:2) to be said by him principally not of bodily foods but of God's words that nourish the soul: the most faithful and most perfect can partake of all — whom he indicates through the 'One believes he may eat all things' — while the weaker and more imperfect begins with simpler lessons, which do not strongly impart vigor — whom, wishing to mark him, he calls 'the weak eats herbs.'

And I take what is said with Solomon in the Proverbs to teach that he who, through simplicity, cannot hold the more vigorous and greater doctrines — yet does not think amiss — is better than the readier, sharper man who charges more greatly upon realities but does not make plain the word of the peace and harmony of all. The wording runs thus: 'Better a portion of herbs with friendship and grace than a calf from the stall with hatred.' (Proverbs 15:17) Often, at any rate, we have welcomed a private and simpler feast with a good conscience — entertained by those who could set nothing more before us — rather than loftiness of words raised 'against the knowledge of God,' proclaiming with great plausibility a doctrine foreign to the Father who gave 'the law and the prophets,' the Father of our Lord Jesus. That our soul, then, may not sicken for lack of foods, nor die to God 'by famine of the Lord's word,' let us ask of the Father the living bread — who is the same as the daily — persuaded by our teacher and Savior, believing and living more rightly.

But what the 'daily' is must now be considered. And first know this: that the word 'daily' (epiousios) has been named by no Greek, neither of the wise nor in common private usage — but seems coined by the evangelists. At any rate Matthew and Luke agreed upon it, bringing it forth nowise differing. The translators of the Hebrew did the like in other cases too. For what Greek ever used the appellation 'give ear' (enotizou), or the 'be eared' (akoutistheti) for 'receive with ears and make hearing'? Like the appellation 'daily' (epeousion) is what stands written with Moses, spoken by God: 'But you shall be to me' 'a peculiar people' (periousios). And each word seems to me made from 'substance' (ousia) — the one declaring the bread that contributes toward substance, the other signifying the people concerned with substance and sharing in it.

Now 'substance,' properly, is conceived by those who say the subsistence of the incorporeal is prior: after the incorporeal — things stably having being, admitting neither addition nor suffering subtraction (for this is peculiar to bodies, about which increase and wasting occur, since they are fluent, needing the incoming sustainer that nourishes; if more comes in seasonally than flows away, increase occurs; if less, decrease; and perhaps some receive the incoming thing not at all, in unmixed, if I may so speak ... ). But by those who deem substance consequent, with bodies prior, its definitions are these: substance is either the first matter of beings, and that from which beings come; or the matter of bodies, and that from which bodies come; or of named things, and that from which named things come; or the first substrate without quality; or what pre-subsists for beings; or what receives all changes and alterations, itself unaltered in its own ratio; or what abides through all alteration and change. On their view substance is both qualityless and unfigured in its own ratio — having no appointed magnitude either — but is set under every quality like a ready place. And 'qualities' they ordinarily call activities and makings — wherein happenings and relations turn out to be; for they say substance shares in none of these in its own ratio, but is ever inseparable from one of them by affection — no less receptive of all the maker's activities, as he makes and changes. For the tone connate with it, pervading through all of every quality, is the cause of the economies about it. Through wholes, then, they call it changeable and through wholes divisible, and say all substance can be mingled with all — united, however.

But since, inquiring concerning substance on account of the 'daily bread' and the peculiar people, we said these things to discern what substance signifies — and bread in what went before was intelligible, which we had to ask — substance akin to the bread must necessarily be conceived: that as bodily bread, dispensed, passes into the body of the nourished and into its substance, so the 'living' bread, 'come down from heaven,' dispensed into mind and soul, may share its own power with the one who offered himself to nourishment from it. And so shall be what we ask: 'daily bread.' And again: as, according to the 'quality' of the 'food' — whether 'solid' and suited to athletes, or milky and herby — the nourished comes to be in diverse power, so it follows that, as God's Word is becomingly given — whether as milk to babes, or as herbs to the sick in season, or as flesh to contenders in season — each of the nourished, by the analogy of the Word to which he offered himself, can do this or that, and become this or that. Yet there is a deemed food that is poisonous, and another that makes sick, and another that cannot even be dispensed — all of which must by analogy be transferred to the diversities of deemed nourishing lessons. Daily bread, then, is what is most fitting to the rational nature and most akin to substance itself — procuring at once health and good habit and strength for the soul, and sharing its own immortality (for God's Word is immortal) with the one who eats it.

This daily bread, then, seems to me called by another name in Scripture 'the tree of life' — toward which he who stretches 'his hand' and takes from it 'shall live forever.' And by a third name this 'tree' is called God's 'wisdom' with Solomon, in these words: 'She is a tree of life to all who cling to her, and safe as upon the Lord to those who lean.' (Proverbs 3:18) And since angels too are nourished by God's wisdom — empowered, from contemplation in truth with wisdom, to perform their own works — it is said in the Psalms that angels too are nourished, with men of God — Hebrews, as they are called — sharing with the angels, and as it were feasting with them. Such is the 'bread of angels man ate.' For let our mind not be so poor as to suppose the angels, who ever partake, are nourished by some bodily bread — the storied bread that came down from heaven upon those who left Egypt — with the Hebrews sharing this same bread with the angels, God's ministering spirits.

It is not untimely, as we seek the 'daily bread' and the 'tree of life' and God's wisdom — the common food of holy men and angels — to attend also to the three men recorded in Genesis, brought down with Abraham and partaking of three measures of 'fine flour' kneaded into loaves: lest these things be said barely tropically, since the saints can at times share intelligible and rational food not only with men but even with diviner powers — whether for their benefit or to display what most nourishing things they have been able to procure for themselves — with the angels rejoicing and nourished in such display, and becoming readier to co-work in every way and to breathe together thereafter toward the grasp of more and greater things, upon the nourishing lessons furnished beforehand to the rest — he having gladdened and, if I may so speak, nursed them. It is no wonder if a man nourishes angels — when even Christ confesses he stands at the 'door' and knocks, that, entering with the one who opened to him, he may sup 'with him' from that one's goods, and afterwards himself share his own with the one who first feasted the Son of God, according to his own power.

Of the daily bread, then, he who partakes, strengthening his 'heart,' becomes a son of God; but he who shares in the 'dragon' is no other than the intelligible Ethiopian — changing, through the dragon's ... , even himself into a serpent — so that, reproached by the Word, even if he says he wishes to be baptized, he hears: 'Brood of vipers, who warned you to flee from the coming wrath?' (Matthew 3:7) And David says this concerning the dragon's body feasted upon by the Ethiopians: 'Thou didst crush the heads of the dragons upon the water; thou didst break the serpent's head in pieces; thou gavest him for food to the Ethiopian peoples.' But if it is no absurdity — with the Son of God substantially subsisting, and the Opponent also subsisting — that each becomes food, one to this one, one to that — why do we hesitate to accept, for all powers better and worse, and for men, that each of us can be nourished from all these? At any rate Peter, about to share with the centurion Cornelius and those gathered with him in Caesarea, and after this to share God's words with the nations too, sees 'heaven opened' and a 'vessel let down by four beginnings,' (Acts 10:11) 'wherein were all the quadrupeds and creeping things and wild beasts of the earth' (Acts 10:12) — and is bid 'rise,' sacrifice, and eat. And when, begging off, he said, 'Thou knowest that never did common or unclean enter my mouth,' (Acts 10:14) he is ordered to 'call no man common or unclean' — since what God cleansed Peter must not make common. For the saying runs: 'What God cleansed, make thou not common.' (Acts 10:15) So the clean food and the unclean, distinguished in the Mosaic law under names of many animals, referring to the diverse characters of the rationals, teaches that these are nourishing to us, these contrariwise — until God, cleansing all, makes all nourishing, or those 'from every nation.'

With these things so, and so great a difference of foods, one beyond all those named is the daily bread — concerning which we must pray to be counted worthy of it, and, nourished by the Word, who 'in the beginning' is 'toward God,' to be made godlike. But someone will say the 'daily' (epiousion) is formed from 'coming upon' (epienai) — so that we are commanded to ask the bread proper to the coming age, which God, taking beforehand, may already grant us: so that what is, as it were, to be given tomorrow be given us 'today' — 'today' taken of the present age, 'tomorrow' of the coming. But since the former interpretation is better, so far as I am judge, let us examine what lies beside it: the 'today' with Matthew, or the 'day by day' written with Luke. It is the custom in many places of Scripture to call the whole age 'today' — as 'this is the father of the Moabites unto this day,' (Genesis 19:37) and 'this is the father of the Ammonites unto this day,' (Genesis 19:38) and 'this saying was spread abroad among the Jews unto this day,' (Matthew 28:15) and in the Psalms, 'Today, if you hear his voice, harden not your hearts.' (Psalm 95:7) And with Jesus it is said most plainly thus: 'Depart not from the Lord in the today's days.' And if 'today' is this whole age, perhaps 'yesterday' is the age gone by. Which we have taken to be said in the Psalms and with Paul in Hebrews: in the Psalms thus — 'A thousand years in thy sight are as the day of yesterday, which is past' (Psalms 90:4) (whatever the famed millennium is, likened to the 'yesterday' day, differing from the 'today'); and with the Apostle it is written: 'Jesus Christ, yesterday and today, the same, and unto the ages.' And it is no wonder that to God the whole age has the ratio of one day with us — I suppose, of even less.

And it must be examined whether the words of the feasts recorded by 'days' or 'months' or 'seasons' or 'years' or 'assemblies' refer to ages. For if 'the law has a shadow of the coming things,' the many sabbaths must be a 'shadow' of many days, and the new moons, occurring through temporal intervals — I know not with what moon attending what sun they are performed. And if the first 'month,' and the tenth day 'unto the fourteenth,' and the feast of unleavened from the fourteenth 'unto the twenty-first,' contain a 'shadow of coming things' — 'who is wise, and' to such degree a 'friend' of God, as to see, of more months, the first, and its tenth day, and what follows? And what need to speak of the feast of seven weeks of days, and of the seventh month — whose new moon is a day 'of trumpets,' and whose tenth day is a day 'of atonement' — known to the God alone who legislated them? And who has so held the mind of Christ as to grasp the seventh years of the Hebrew slaves' freedom, and the 'release' of debts, and rest from tilling the holy land? And there is one higher than the feast through seven years, called Jubilee — which, even to imagine in part, or to grasp plainly that its laws shall be fulfilled as true, belongs to none except the one who contemplated the Father's counsel concerning the ordinance in all the ages, according to his 'unsearchable' 'judgments' and his untraceable ways.

Often it came upon me to wonder, comparing two apostolic sayings, how it is the 'consummation of the ages,' at which Jesus 'has been manifested for the annulling of sins' — if ages are to come after this one. The sayings run thus: in Hebrews, 'But now once, at the consummation of the ages, he has been manifested, for the annulling of sins through his sacrifice'; in Ephesians, 'that in the coming ages he might show the exceeding riches of his grace in kindness toward us.' (Ephesians 2:7) Pondering such greatness, I suppose that, as the last month is the consummation of the year — after which another month's beginning sets in — so perhaps, with many ages completing, as it were, a year of ages, the present age is the consummation, after which certain coming ages shall set in, whose beginning is the coming age — and in those coming ages God shall display the riches 'of his grace in kindness' — with the most sinful, even the blasphemer against the Holy Spirit, held fast by sin in the whole present age, and from the beginning to the end, to be dispensed in the coming age afterward — how, I know not.

He, then, who saw these things, and conceived in mind a week of ages — to contemplate a holy sabbatism — and a month of ages — to see God's holy new moon — and a year of ages — to understand together the year's feasts, when every 'male' must appear 'before the Lord God' — and the proportionate years of such ages — to grasp the holy seventh year — and seven sevens of ages — to hymn the so-great Lawgiver — having examined how he can fuss over the least portion of an hour of the day of so great an age, will do everything, that, made worthy by preparation here of obtaining the daily bread, he may receive it on the 'today' day — with the 'day by day' already becoming plain from what went before. For to the God who is from boundless to boundless, the one who prays concerning not only the 'today' but in a way the 'today' of the 'day by day' — from what he can contemplate — 'beyond all measure above what we ask or conceive' — shall be able to receive, if I may speak so hyperbolically, even 'what eye saw not' and 'what ear heard not' and 'what went not up upon man's heart.'

And these things too seem to me most necessary to examine, that both the 'today' be understood and the 'day by day,' when we pray that the 'daily bread' 'be given us' from his Father. But if in the last book we shall first examine the 'our' — since it is said not 'Give us this day our daily bread' but 'Our daily bread give us day by day' — yet we must examine how this bread is 'ours.' The Apostle teaches that 'whether life or death, or things present or things to come — all' are the saints'. Concerning which there is no need to speak at present.

before: 'And forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors' (Matthew 6:12) — or as Luke has it, 'And forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us.' (Romans 13:7–8) Concerning debts, the Apostle says: 'Render to all their dues: tribute to whom tribute, fear to whom fear, tax to whom tax, honor to whom honor. Owe no one anything, except to love one another.' (1 Samuel 2:25) We owe, then — holding certain duties — not only in giving, but in gentle speech too, and in certain works; and we owe a certain disposition toward them. These debts we either pay, by performing what the divine law commands, or, by despising the wholesome word, not paying, we remain in owing.

The like must be conceived for debts toward brothers — both those reborn with us in Christ by the word of godliness, and those of our womb or our father. There is a debt toward citizens too, and another common one toward all men — toward strangers in particular, and in particular toward those of a father's age — and another toward some, whom it is reasonable to honor as sons or as brothers. He who does not see that what is owed to brothers is performed remains a debtor of what he did not do. And he — if, when men cast upon us some of our failings, from the philanthropic spirit of wisdom — the debt grows greater. But we owe to ourselves too: to use the body thus — not to wear out the body's flesh by love of pleasure; and to bring this care to the soul, and make provision for the mind's keenness, and for speech, that it be stingless and useful and nowise idle. And when we do not do what is owed by us to ourselves, our liability becomes heavier.

And beyond all these, as God's 'workmanship' and creation, we owe him a certain disposition kept toward him, and love 'from the whole heart' 'and from the whole strength' 'and from the whole mind.' If we do not accomplish these, we remain debtors to God, sinning against the Lord. And who shall pray for us concerning these? 'For if a man sinning sin against a man, they shall pray for him; but if he sin against the Lord, who shall pray for him?' (Ephesians 4:30) — as Eli says in First Kingdoms. But with Christ having bought us with his own blood, we are debtors — as every slave is debtor to his buyer for so great a sum given for him. And we have a debt toward 'the Holy Spirit' too — paid when we grieve him not, 'whereby' we were 'sealed unto the day of redemption' — and, not grieving him, bear the fruits we are required to bear, with him present in us and quickening our soul. And if we know not exactly who is each one's angel, 'beholding' in the heavens the Father's 'face' — yet to each who oversees himself it becomes plain that to him too we are debtors of certain things. And if we are 'in a theater of the world and angels and men,' (Matthew 18:19 (angels)) know that, as in a theater one is debtor to say or do such things in sight of the spectators — which, if he do not, he is punished as having insulted the whole theater — so we owe 'to' the whole 'world' 'and' to all, angels and the race of men, the things we shall learn from wisdom if we will.

But apart from these more general debts, there is a debt of a widow cared for by the church, and another of a deacon, and another of a presbyter — and a bishop's debt is heaviest, exacted by the Savior of the whole church, and avenged if unpaid. And the Apostle named a common debt of man and wife, saying: 'Let the husband render the debt to the wife, and likewise the wife to the husband' (1 Corinthians 7:3) — adding, 'Defraud not one another.' And why must I say what readers of this writing can gather for themselves from what is said — how many debts, either not paying, we shall be held, or paying, be freed? Only, living in this life, there is no hour of night or day without owing.

But in owing, one either pays or keeps back the debt. In this life one can pay; one can also keep back. Some owe nothing to anyone; some, paying most, owe little; some, paying little, owe more; and perhaps there is one who, paying nothing, owes all. And he who pays all, so as to owe nothing, succeeds in this in time — needing forgiveness for former debts. Which forgiveness he who has been zealous, from some time, to become such as to owe nothing of what befalls him, as unpaid, may reasonably obtain. And these lawless activities, imprinted on the ruling faculty, become the 'handwriting against us' by which we shall be judged — as books, as it were, written by all hands, to be produced when 'we shall all stand before the tribunal' (1 Corinthians 7:3–5) 'of Christ, that each may receive the things through the body, according to what he did, whether good or bad.' (Colossians 2:14) To these debts belongs also what is said in Proverbs: 'Give not thyself for surety, ashamed of face; for if thou hast not whence to pay, they shall take thy mattress from under thy sides.' (2 Corinthians 5:10)

And if we owe to so many, then certainly some owe to us: some owe us as men, others as citizens, others as fathers, some as sons — and after these, wives to husbands as husbands, or friends to friends as friends. When, then, some of our many debtors behave more weakly concerning the payment of what is due to us, we shall do more humanely if we bear it with forgetfulness of wrongs toward them, remembering our own debts — how many we often passed by, not only toward men but toward God himself. For remembering that, being debtors, we did not pay but kept back, with time passing in which we should have done such things toward our neighbor, we shall be gentler toward those who owed even to us and did not pay the debt — especially if we forget not what was presumptuously done against the Divine by us, and the 'iniquity against the height' spoken by us, whether in ignorance of the truth or in displeasure at the circumstances befalling us.

But if we will not become gentler toward those indebted to us, we shall suffer what befell the one who forgave not his fellow-slave the 'hundred denarii' — who, forgiven according to the parable lying in the Gospel, was seized, and his master exacts the forgiven sums, saying to him: 'Wicked and slothful slave, oughtest thou not to have pitied thy fellow-slave, as I pitied thee? Cast him into prison, till he pay all that is owed.' (Proverbs 22:26–27) And the Lord adds to this: 'So also shall my heavenly Father do to you, if you forgive not each one his brother from your hearts.' (Matthew 18:23–35) Yet they say we must forgive the repentant among those who sinned against us, even if our debtor do this often: 'For,' he says, 'if seven times a day thy brother sin against thee,' (Luke 17:4) and seven times turn, saying 'I repent,' thou shalt forgive him. It is not we who are harsh toward the unrepentant — such are harsh to themselves: 'for he who casts off discipline hates himself.' (John 20:23) Yet even for such, healing must by every means be sought to come upon the wholly perverted — so as not even to perceive his own evils, but to be drunk with a drunkenness more deadly than 'from wine': the drunkenness from the stupor of wickedness.

But Luke, saying 'Forgive us our sins' — since sins are debts of debtors who owe and pay not — says the same as Matthew, who seems to give no place to one who wishes to forgive only repentant debtors, since the Savior legislated that we must add in prayer: 'For we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us.' (Luke 11:4) Yet we all have authority to forgive sins against us — plain from both the 'as we also forgive our debtors' and the 'for we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us.' (Job 1:5) But he who is breathed upon by Jesus as the apostles were, and can be known 'by their fruits' as having received the Holy Spirit, and become spiritual by being led by the Spirit in the manner of a son of God for each thing to be done according to reason — forgives whatever God forgives, and retains the unhealable sins, serving, as the prophets did in speaking not their own things but the divine will's to God — so he too serves the God alone who has authority to forgive.

The voices in John's Gospel concerning the apostles' forgiveness run thus: 'Receive the Holy Spirit. Whosesoever sins you forgive, they are forgiven them; whosesoever you retain, they are retained.' (John 20:23) But if anyone takes these without examination, one might blame the apostles for not forgiving all, that all be forgiven — but retaining some sins, so that through them they are retained with God too. It is useful to take an example from the Law, to understand the forgiveness of men's sins wrought by men under God for men. The priests according to the Law are forbidden to offer sacrifice for certain sins, that the trespasses for which the sacrifices are made be forgiven. And surely the priest, having authority for the offering concerning involuntary or ... trespasses, does not already offer whole-burnt-offering and sin-offering for adultery or willful murder or any graver fall. So too the apostles, and those likened to the apostles — priests under the 'great' 'High Priest,' having received knowledge of God's healing — know, taught by the Spirit, for what they must offer sacrifices of sins, and when, and in what manner — and know for what they must not do this. At any rate the priest Eli, knowing his sons Hophni and Phinehas sinning, as able to co-work nothing toward forgiveness of sins for them, confesses despair that this shall be, through what he says: 'If a man sinning sin against a man, they shall pray for him; but if he sin against the Lord, who shall pray for him?'

I know not how some, permitting themselves things beyond priestly worth — perhaps not even exact about priestly knowledge — boast as able to forgive idolatries, adulteries, and fornications too — to loose, through their prayer for the daring, even the 'sin unto death.' For they do not read the 'There is a sin unto death; I do not say that one should ask concerning it.' Nor must we pass over in silence most manly Job, offering sacrifice for his sons, saying: 'Lest my sons in their mind conceived evil against God' — for concerning doubtful cases, whether sin was sinned — and these not even reaching the lips — he offers the sacrifice.

The priests according to the Law are forbidden to offer sacrifice for certain sins, that the trespasses for which the sacrifices are made be forgiven. So too the apostles, and those likened to the apostles — priests under the 'great' 'High Priest,' having received knowledge of God's healing — know, taught by the Spirit, for what they must offer sacrifices of sins, and when, and in what manner — and know for what they must not do this. I know not how some, permitting themselves things beyond priestly worth — perhaps not even exact about priestly knowledge — boast as able to forgive idolatries, adulteries, and fornications too — to loose, through their prayer for the daring, even the 'sin unto death.' For they do not read the 'There is a sin unto death; I do not say that one should ask concerning it.' Nor must we pass over in silence most manly Job, offering sacrifice for his sons, saying: 'Lest my sons in their mind conceived evil against God' — for concerning doubtful cases, whether sin was sinned — and these not even reaching the lips — he offers the sacrifice.
