before: 'Our Father who art in the heavens.' (Philippians 3:20) It is worth watching more exactly whether the old covenant, as it is called, has anywhere in it a prayer of someone calling God Father. For at present, examining as we can, we have not found one. We do not say this — that God has not been called Father, or that those deemed to have believed God have not been named sons of God — but that in prayer we have not yet found the frankness announced by the Savior concerning naming God Father. That God has been called Father, and that those who have come to the word of God are sons, can be seen in many places — as in Deuteronomy: 'Thou hast forsaken God who begot thee, and forgotten God who nourishes thee' (Deuteronomy 32:6,18,20); and again: 'Is not this thy Father who bought thee and made thee and created thee?' (Isaiah 1:2); and again: 'Sons, in whom there is no faith'; and in Isaiah: 'Sons I begot and raised, but they rejected me' (Malachi 1:6); and in Malachi: 'A son shall glorify his father, and a servant his master. And if I am a Father, where is my glory? And if I am a Master, where is my fear?' (Galatians 4:1–5)

If, then, God is called Father, and those begotten by the word of faith in him are sons, yet the firm and unfallen character of sonship is not to be seen among the ancients. At any rate the very passages we set out show those called sons to be blameworthy — since, according to the Apostle, 'while the heir is a child, he differs nothing from a slave, though lord of all, but is under guardians and stewards until the term appointed by the father.' (Romans 8:15–17) But 'the fullness of time' lies in the sojourn of our Lord Jesus Christ, when those who will receive the adoption — as Paul teaches in these words: 'For you received not a spirit of slavery unto fear, but you received a spirit of adoption, wherein we cry: Abba, Father.' (John 1:12) And in John: 'But as many as received him, he gave them authority to become children of God — to those who believe in his name.' (1 John 3:8–9) And that is why, concerning those born of God, we have learned through the 'spirit of adoption' in John's catholic epistle that 'everyone born of God does no sin, for his seed abides in him' (1 Corinthians 12:3) — and he cannot sin, because he is born of God.

But if we consider what 'When you pray, say: Father' — as written with Luke — is, we shall hesitate, unless we have become genuine sons, to bring this voice to him — lest, besides our other sins, we become liable to a charge of impiety as well. What I say is like this. Paul says in First Corinthians: 'No one can say: Lord Jesus, except in the Holy Spirit; and no one speaking in the Spirit of God says: Anathema Jesus' (Romans 10:10) — naming the Holy Spirit and the Spirit of God as the same. But what saying 'in the Holy Spirit' 'Lord Jesus' is, is not at all plain — when myriads of hypocrites and still more heterodox utter the voice, and at times even demons, overcome by the power in the name. No one will dare to declare that any of these says 'Lord Jesus' 'in the Holy Spirit.' So they would not even be shown to say 'Lord Jesus' — only those who say it from their disposition, serving the word of God and proclaiming no other Lord in whatever they do: that is 'Lord Jesus.' And if such are those who say 'Lord Jesus,' then perhaps everyone who sins, outlawing the divine Word by transgression, cries out by his works: 'Anathema Jesus.' As, then, the one so disposed says 'Lord Jesus,' and the one oppositely disposed says 'Anathema Jesus' — so everyone 'born of God' 'and doing no sin,' by sharing God's seed, which turns him from all sin — by what he does he says 'Our Father who art in the heavens,' with his own spirit bearing witness with their spirit 'that they are children of God' — and his heirs, 'joint-heirs with Christ,' since suffering together they reasonably hope to be glorified together. And lest such say 'Our Father' only by halves, with their works their heart too — the fountain and source of good works — 'believes unto righteousness,' with which the mouth in agreement confesses 'unto salvation.'

Every work of theirs, then, and word and thought, formed by the Only-begotten Word after himself, has imitated the 'image of the invisible God' and become 'after the image of him who created' — who makes 'his sun rise' 'on evil and good' and sends rain 'on righteous and unrighteous' — so that 'the image of the heavenly' is in them, since he is the image of God. Being 'images,' then, of the Image — the Image being Son — the saints wipe off(?) sonship(?) — not only by becoming conformed in body to the body of Christ's glory, but also while being in 'the body.' And they become conformed to the One in the 'body of glory' by being 'transformed by the renewal of the mind.' (Colossians 1:15) But if such say 'Our Father who art in the heavens' in all things, then plainly 'he who does sin' — as John says in the catholic epistle — 'is of the devil, for the devil sins from the beginning.' (Matthew 5:45) And as God's 'seed,' abiding in the one 'born of God,' causes the inability to sin in the one formed after the Only-begotten Word — so in everyone who 'does sin' there is the devil's 'seed,' so far as it is present in the soul, not permitting its possessor to succeed. But since 'for this the Son of God was manifested, that he might loose the works of the devil,' (1 Corinthians 15:49) it is possible, by the visitation of God's Word upon our soul — the 'devil's' works being loosed — for the evil 'seed' implanted in us to be wiped away, and for us to become 'children of God.'

Let us not suppose, then, that we are taught to say phrases at some appointed season of praying. If we understood what was examined before about praying 'without ceasing,' our whole life — as of those who pray 'without ceasing' — should say 'Our Father who art in the heavens,' having our 'citizenship' in no way on earth but in every way 'in the heavens,' since we are thrones of God, because God's kingdom is founded in all who bear 'the image of the heavenly' and have therefore become heavenly.

before: 'Hallowed be thy name.' When prayer sets forth something as not yet come to be, concerning which one prays — or, having obtained this, asks that it remain and be kept — it is plain, on the face of the words here, that we are commanded to say, in Matthew and in Luke, 'Hallowed be thy name,' as though the Father's name were not yet hallowed. And how, one might say, does a man deem it worthy that God's 'name' be hallowed, as though unhallowed? What the Father's 'name' is, and what hallowing it is, let us consider.

A 'name,' then, is a summary appellation, indicative of the proper quality of the named — as, say, some proper quality of Paul the apostle: one of his soul, whereby it is of such a sort; another of his mind, whereby he is contemplative; another of his body, whereby it is of such a sort. What is peculiar in these qualities, then, and unconfused toward another — for there is no other in being exactly unvarying from Paul — is declared by the appellation 'Paul.' But in men, whose proper qualities change, as it were, the names too are soundly changed according to Scripture: for when the quality of 'Abram' changed, he was called 'Abraham'; and when Simon's did, he was named 'Peter'; and the persecutor of Jesus, 'Saul,' was addressed as 'Paul.' But with God — who is himself unchangeable and unalterable, ever the same — there is ever one, as it were, name upon him too: the 'I am' spoken in Exodus, if we may so speak. Since, then, we all suppose something concerning God, conceiving whatever notions about him — but all do not grasp what he is (for rare, and, if one must say so, rarer than the rare, are those who grasp his holiness in all things) — we are fittingly taught that our inner conception of God become holy, that we may see his holiness: creating and providing and judging and choosing and forsaking, accepting and rejecting, counting worthy of honor and chastising each according to worth.

For in these and like things, if I may so speak, is characteristically stamped God's proper quality — which I take to be called God's 'name' in the Scriptures: in Exodus, 'Thou shalt not take the name of the Lord thy God in vain' (Exodus 20:7); in Deuteronomy, 'Let my utterance wait as rain; let my words come down as dew, as shower upon grass and as snowfall upon herb: for I have called the name of the Lord' (Deuteronomy 32:2); in the Psalms, 'They shall remember thy name in every generation and generation.' (Exodus 20:7) For he who misfits his conception of God takes 'the name of the Lord God' 'in vain'; and he who can utter rain that co-works with his hearers for the fruit-bearing of their souls, and bring forth words like dew — comforting words — and by the rush of well-built speeches bring upon his hearers most profitable rain or most useful snowfall — can do these things for this reason. Having conceived this, he calls upon himself the one who begs God, who perfects, the true giver of the things aforesaid. And everyone who makes plain the things concerning God reminds rather than teaches — even if he seems to hear from someone or thinks he finds the mysteries of godliness.

As, then, the pray-er must here understand to ask that God's 'name' be hallowed, so in the Psalms 'Let us exalt his name together' is said — with the prophet commanding, in all harmony, in the same mind and the same judgment, to arrive beforehand at the true and lofty knowledge of God's proper quality. For this is exalting God's 'name' 'together': when one, having received of divinity's effluence by conceiving from God and getting mastery over his enemies, gladdened at a fall they cannot effect, exalts the very power of God of which he has shared. Which is declared in the twenty-ninth Psalm through 'I will exalt thee, O Lord, for thou hast upheld me, and hast not gladdened my enemies over me.' (Deuteronomy 32:2) And one exalts God by consecrating him a house in oneself — since even the psalm's title runs thus: 'A Psalm of a song, for the dedication of the house, of David.' (Psalm 44:18 (LXX))

But Tatian, not observing that the 'let it be' does not always signify the optative but sometimes the imperative too, most impiously supposed concerning the God who said 'Let there be light' — that he prayed rather than commanded the light to come to be. Does he pray, for the sake of standing firmly, that 'the water below heaven be gathered into one gathering' (Psalm 29:1)? And if, on his own showing, praying about these things — spoken with imperative appellations — is absurd, why not say the like concerning the 'Let there be light': that it was spoken not optatively but imperatively? I deemed it necessary, since a prayer spoken in imperative voices has come up, to recall his misreadings — for the sake of those deceived who have received his impious teaching, of whom we ourselves once had experience.

before: 'Thy will be done, as in heaven, also upon earth.' (Matthew 6:10) Luke, after the 'Thy kingdom come,' passed over these words in silence and goes on: 'Our daily bread give us day by day.' (Matthew 6:11) So let us examine the words we set first, as lying in Matthew alone, in sequence with what went before. Still being 'on earth,' those who pray conceive that God's 'will' has come to be 'in heaven' among all the dwellers in heaven; and we pray that God's 'will' may come to be in us, who are 'still on earth,' in all things as with them. Which shall happen when we do nothing against his 'will.' And when God's 'will' — 'as in heaven' — is accomplished in us who are 'on earth,' we who are likened to those in the heavens, having borne, like them, 'the image of the heavenly,' (1 Corinthians 15:48–49) shall inherit the 'kingdom of the heavens' (Job 40:19 (LXX)) — we who pray on earth that we, having become 'in heaven,' be likened to them.

But according to Matthew alone, the 'as in heaven and on earth' (Matthew 6:10) can be taken in common — so that what is enjoined upon us to say in prayer runs thus: 'Hallowed be thy name' (1 Corinthians 15:50) 'as in heaven and on earth'; 'Thy kingdom come' 'as in heaven and on earth' (Job 40:19); 'Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth.' (Matthew 6:10) For God's 'name' has been hallowed among those 'in heaven,' and God's 'kingdom' has stood in them, and God's 'will' has come to be in them — all of which is lacking to us who are 'on earth,' but can come to be ours as we make ourselves worthy to obtain God's hearing concerning all these things.

But someone may ask, saying 'Thy will be done, as in heaven and on earth' (Matthew 6:10): how has God's 'will' come to be 'in heaven,' where 'the spiritual hosts of wickedness' are, on account of which God's 'sword shall be drunk' 'in heaven'? And if we so pray that God's 'will' come to be 'on' 'earth' as it is done 'in heaven,' might we unawares be praying that contrary things also remain 'on earth' — since these too come from heaven — with many base things coming to be 'on earth' through the inferior 'spiritual hosts of wickedness' that are 'in the heavenly places'? One who allegorizes heaven, saying it is Christ, and earth the church — for who is so 'a throne' of the Father as Christ? And what 'footstool of God's feet' as the church? — will easily loose the questions, saying each member of the church must so receive the paternal 'will' as Christ received it — who came to do his Father's 'will' and perfected it all. For it is possible, joined to him, to become 'one spirit' with him, thereby receiving the 'will' as one: as it is perfected 'in heaven,' so may it be perfected 'also on earth.' For 'he who is joined to the Lord,' according to Paul, 'is one spirit.' And I suppose this interpretation will prove not contemptible to one who considers it more exactly.

But one who opposes it will set beside it what was said at the end of this Gospel, after the resurrection, by the Lord to the eleven disciples: 'All authority has been given me, as in heaven, also on earth.' (Matthew 28:18) For having authority over those 'in heaven' — he says he has received in addition that 'on earth': those 'in heaven' having been enlightened even before by the Word, and at the 'consummation of the age' those 'on earth' too, through the authority given to the Son of God, imitating the things accomplished 'in heaven,' over which the Savior received authority. As it were, then, through our prayers he wishes to take those discipled to him as co-workers with the Father — that, as the things 'in heaven' are subjected to truth and the Word, so the things 'on earth,' set right through the authority he received 'as in heaven and on earth,' may bring the ruled to a blessed end. And one who calls the Savior heaven and earth the church — 'the firstborn of all creation,' in whom the Father rests as upon a throne, calling him heaven — would find the 'man' whom he put on, made his own by that power through 'humbling himself' and becoming 'obedient unto death,' saying after the resurrection the 'All authority has been given me, as in heaven and on earth' (Colossians 1:15) — the authority 'in heaven,' as of the things indwelling the Only-begotten, received by the man according to the Savior, that he may share it with him, mingled with his divinity and united to him.

But since the second interpretation does not yet loose the difficulties concerning how God's 'will' is 'in heaven,' with the spiritual hosts 'of wickedness' 'in the heavenly places' wrestling against those 'on earth' — from that side it will be possible to loose the question thus: that, as it is not by place but by choice that one 'on earth,' having his 'citizenship in heaven' and treasuring 'in heaven,' with his heart 'in heaven,' bearing 'the image of the heavenly,' is no longer 'of the earth' nor of the 'below' 'world,' but of heaven and of the better, 'heavenly' 'world' beyond this — so too the 'spiritual hosts of wickedness' still lingering 'in the heavenly places,' having their 'citizenship on earth,' plotting against men through what they wrestle, treasuring on earth, bearing 'the image of the earthy' — 'he who is the beginning of the Lord's creation, made to be mocked by the angels' — are not heavenly nor in the heavens, because of their wretched disposition. When, then, it is said 'Thy will be done, as in heaven, also on earth,' (Philippians 2:8) those must not be reckoned to be 'in heaven' at all — having fallen in mind with him who fell 'from heaven' 'like lightning.'

And perhaps, when our Savior commands that we must pray that the Father's 'will' come to be 'as in heaven' 'so also on earth,' he does not at all command that our prayers concern those in the place 'above,' that they be likened to those in the heavenly place. His injunction of prayer is, for one who wishes all things 'on earth' — that is, the worse things, made like to earthly things — to be likened to the better, to all who have 'their citizenship in heaven,' who have all become heaven. For the sinner, wherever he is, is 'earth' — who, unless he repent, shall come to his kindred earth. But he who does God's 'will' and disobeys none of the saving spiritual laws is heaven. Whether, then, we are still 'earth' through sin, let us pray that God's 'will' extend over us too, setting right, as it already reached those before us who are heaven or were heaven; or whether we are reckoned by God no longer earth but heaven already, let us ask that 'on earth' too, as in 'heaven' — I mean, among the worse — God's 'will' be fulfilled, unto the heaven-making, if I may so speak, of earth, so that earth be earth no longer, but all things become heaven. For if God's 'will,' as 'in heaven' in the senses interpreted, come to be 'also on earth,' earth shall not remain earth. As if I spoke more plainly on another example: if God's 'will,' as it has come to be upon the temperate, so come to be also upon the intemperate, the intemperate shall be temperate; or as God's 'will' has come to be upon the righteous, if it so come to be also upon the unrighteous, the unrighteous shall be righteous. That is why, if God's 'will,' as it has come to be 'in heaven,' come to be 'also on earth,' we shall all be heaven — with the unprofitable flesh and its kindred blood unable to inherit 'God's kingdom,' but to be said to inherit if they 'change from flesh and earth and dust and blood to the heavenly substance.' (Philippians 3:20)

before: If Jesus prays, and prays not in vain — obtaining what he asks through praying, which perhaps he would not have received without prayer — who of us neglects praying? Mark says: 'Rising very early in the night he went out and departed to a desert place, and there prayed.' (Mark 1:35) Luke: 'And it came to pass, as he was praying in a certain place' (Luke 11:1) — and elsewhere: 'And he spent the night in the prayer of God.' (Luke 6:12) John records his prayer, saying: 'These things Jesus spoke, and lifting his eyes to heaven he said: Father, the hour has come; glorify Your Son, that Your Son may glorify You.' (John 17:1) And 'I knew that You always hear me,' (Esther 4:16) recorded by him as spoken by the Lord, shows that always praying he is always heard.

Why list those benefited by God for praying in the 'what' manner, heard obtaining what they prayed? Hannah, believing though barren to pray — whereby she was wholly deemed worthy to bear Samuel the prophet, numbered after Moses. before: Since, as we said in what went before, the one who prays must first be established — how disposed and in what condition — and only then pray, let us see, before the prayer that lies in Matthew, the words spoken about it by our Savior, which run thus: 'When you pray, you shall not be as the hypocrites; for they love to pray standing in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets, that they may be seen by men. In many places, then, our Savior is seen pressing against ambition as a passion that destroys; which he has done here also, turning men away from performing a hypocrite's work at the season of prayer. For it is a hypocrite's work to want to preen oneself before men for piety or for fellowship. But we must remember the 'How can you believe, who receive glory from men, and seek not the glory that comes from the only God?' (John 5:44) — and despise all glory from men, even if it is thought to come of the good — and seek the sovereign and true glory, the glory from the only God, who becomingly glorifies, beyond the worth of the glorified, the one worthy of glory. Even what was thought good and praiseworthy is polluted when deemed to be done — when we do it 'that we may be glorified by men' or 'that we may be seen by men.' That is why no recompense from God follows upon it. For every word of Jesus is unlying — and, if one must force the saying, becomes more unlying still when spoken with his customary oath. He says of those who do good for show to win human glory, or who pray 'in the synagogues and on the corners of the streets' (Luke 16:25) 'that they may be seen by men,' the same thing: 'Amen, I say to you: they have received their reward.' For everyone who lives for pleasure, loving the roomy way, has fallen out of the narrow and straitened way of Jesus Christ, which has not even a chance bend, and is nowhere at all cornered.

before: It seems to me, further, having discussed the places of prayer, not to end the word here. Four places, I take it, must be outlined, which I found scattered in the Scriptures — and a prayer must be bodied together for each after these. The places are these: according to power, words of doxology must be said at the prayer's beginning and preface — with God glorified through Christ, hymned together in the Holy Spirit; and after this each must rank common thanksgivings — bringing, upon the thanksgiving, benefits toward many, and what he individually obtained from God; and after thanksgiving, I take one must become embittered over one's own sins, accusing them through confession and asking healing for them and forgiveness from God; and to this, I take it, must be joined the request for great and heavenly things — one's own and general, and for kin and dearest. And upon all, the prayer must rest in God's doxology through Christ in the Holy Spirit.

These places, as we foretold, are found dispersed in the Scriptures: the doxology-place, in the hundred-and-third Psalm, in these words — 'O Lord my God, thou art magnified exceedingly; confession and majesty thou didst put on, who wrappest light as a garment, who stretchest heaven as a hide, who roofest his upper chambers in waters, who makest clouds his footing, who walkest on wings of winds, who makest his angels spirits and his ministers a flame of fire, who foundest earth upon its safety — it shall not bow unto the age of age. before: It seems to me not out of place, after this, for the filling of the problem concerning prayer, to discuss more elementarily the condition and the figure the pray-er must have, and the place where one must pray, and the direction toward which one must look, without any circumstance — and the season fit and choice for prayer, and anything like these. The condition must be laid upon the soul, the figure upon the body. Paul, then — as we said above — sketches the condition in the 'pray' 'without wrath and doubting,' (Psalm 25:4–5 (LXX)) and the figure in the 'lifting holy hands' — which I take him to have received from the Psalms, running thus: 'The lifting of my hands, an evening sacrifice.' (1 Timothy 2:8) Concerning place: 'I will, then, that men pray in every place.' (Psalm 140:2 (LXX)) Concerning direction, in Solomon's Wisdom: 'that it be known that one must outrun the sun unto thy thanksgiving, and meet thee before the light's rising.'

It seems to me, then, that one about to come to prayer — pausing a little and furnishing himself — becomes more attentive and vigorous toward the whole of prayer: casting off all temptation and turmoil of thoughts, reminding himself as far as possible of the greatness to which he approaches, and that it is impious to come to him slack and loose, as it were despising — laying aside all foreign things — so to come to pray: stretching, as it were, his soul before his hands, and straining his mind before his eyes toward God, and before standing, waking his ruling faculty from sloth and stationing it toward the Lord of all — laying aside all remembrance of wrongs toward any deemed to have wronged him, so far as he too wishes God not to remember wrongs against him — who wronged him and sinned against many neighbors, or is conscious of whatever deeds against right reason. Nor must one doubt that, though the body's conditions are myriad, the condition with outstretched hands and uplifted eyes is to be preferred before all — bearing, as it were, upon the body the image of the properties befitting the soul in prayer. And this, I say, must come to be principally without any circumstance. For with circumstance it has been given to pray becomingly at times seated — for some not-contemptible disease of the feet — or even reclining, for fevers or such weaknesses; and for encompassing circumstance — say, if we sail, or business forbids us, withdrawing, to render the owed prayer — one may pray without even pretending to do so.

And kneeling too — when one is about to accuse his own sins before God, entreating healing and forgiveness for them — know that it is a symbol of the fallen and subjected: Paul saying, 'For this I bend my knees to the Father, from whom every family in the heavens and on earth is named.' (Ephesians 3:15) And the intelligible kneeling — so called from falling prostrate to God 'in Jesus' name,' ... each being humbling itself to him — the Apostle seems to me to declare in the 'that in Jesus' name every knee bow, of heavenly and earthly and under-earthly.' For that the heavenly bodies are figured so as to have even bodily knees must hardly be supposed — their bodies being proved spherical by the exact students of these things. And he who will not accept this will accept — unless he blush before reason — the uses of each member: that nothing in them was crafted by God in vain. Either way he trips: whether he says bodily members came to them from God in vain and not for their own work, or says the inward parts and the straight gut perform their own uses even in the heavenly ones. And he shall conduct himself most foolishly if, statue-fashion, one supposes only the surface to be manlike, but no longer the depths. This, I say, examining kneeling, and seeing that 'in Jesus' name every knee shall bow, of heavenly and earthly and under-earthly.' And what stands written in the prophet, 'To me every knee shall bow,' (Philippians 2:10) is the same.

And concerning place, know that every place becomes fit for praying by one who prays well: 'For in every place they bring incense to me,' (Ephesians 3:14) 'says the Lord'; and 'I will, then, that men pray in every place.' (Philippians 2:10) But there is an ordinance, for performing prayers at leisure undistracted — each choosing, of his own house if possible, the more reverend spot — to pray thus, so to speak, in a place: overseeing, besides the general examination of it, whether in this place where he prays anything was ever done amiss and against right reason. For he has made not only himself but even the place of his own prayer such that God's oversight flees thence. And overseeing more fully this place too, I must state an opinion — perhaps weighty, but to the exact trier not contemptible. In the place of not unlawful intercourse, but what by the apostolic word is conceded 'by concession, not by command,' (Psalm 33:8) it must be examined whether it is holy and pure to address God. For to be at leisure 'for prayer' as one must is impossible unless one devote himself to it 'by agreement for a season' (Psalm 25:4–5) — so perhaps concerning the place too, if possible, one must consider.

But a place of prayer has a certain grace toward profit: the place of the believers' assembly together — where, as is likely, angelic powers too oversee the gatherings of believers, and the very power of our Lord and Savior — already, too, holy spirits; and, I suppose, the predeceased — and plainly those still in life, though the how is not easy to say. And concerning angels, reckon thus: if 'the angel of the Lord encamps round them that fear him, and shall deliver them,' (Malachi 1:11) and Jacob speaks truth — not of himself only but of all devoted to the understanding God — saying, 'The angel who delivers me from all evils' (Genesis 48:16) — it is likely, with more genuinely gathered to Christ's glory, that each one's angel encamps 'round' each 'of them that fear,' with that man whom he is trusted to guard and dispense. So that over the saints gathering there is a double church — one of men, one of angels. And if Raphael says of Tobit alone that he brought his prayer 'for a memorial' — and after him Sarah's, who later became his bride through her marriage to Tobias — what must be said, when more accompany in the same place and the same mind, and are bodied together in Christ? And concerning the Lord's power present with the church, Paul says: 'You gathered, and my spirit, with the power of the Lord Jesus' (Psalm 33:8 (LXX)) — as the 'power of the Lord Jesus' joins not with Ephesians only but Corinthians too. And if Paul, still girt with the body, deemed his own spirit to join in Corinth — the blessed departed must not be despaired of reaching the churches in spirit — perhaps more than one in the body. That is why the prayers in them must not be despised — having something choice for the one who genuinely joins them.

But as Jesus' power, and Paul's spirit and his like, and the angels of 'the Lord' 'encamping round' each saint, accompany and join those genuinely assembled — so conjecture whether, if one unworthy of a holy angel, or devoting himself to a diabolical angel by what he sins and transgresses despising God — such a one, though his like be rare, shall not long escape the angels' providence, overseeing the church in service of the divine will, bringing such one's falls to the many's knowledge. But if such become a multitude, gathering in human fellowships and pursuing something more bodily, they shall not be overseen. Which is declared in Isaiah, with the Lord saying: 'Not even if you come to be seen by me' (Genesis 48:16) — 'for,' he says, 'I will turn my eyes from you' — 'and if you multiply supplication, I will not hear you.' (1 Corinthians 5:4) For perhaps, instead of the aforesaid double array of holy men and blessed angels, there comes again a double meeting together of impious men and wicked angels — and of such a gathering it might be said, by holy angels and sacred men: 'I sat not with a council of vanity, and with transgressors I will not enter. I hated the church of evildoers, and with the impious I will not sit.' (Isaiah 1:12–15)

That is why, I suppose, those in Jerusalem and all Judaea, come into more sins, became subject to enemies — abandoned by God and the championing angels and the saints' salvation, the law-forsaking peoples. For so too whole gatherings are at times forsaken, to fall into temptations — that 'even what' they 'seem to have' be 'taken from them': like the cursed fig tree, 'taken from its roots' for giving no fruit to the hungry Jesus — withering, and losing what little vital power in faith they had. This, I take it, I necessarily said, examining a place of prayer, and presenting the choice in place: in the saints' assembly together, and more reverently in the church gathered to the same.

before: Of things moved, some have their mover from outside — like lifeless things held together by mere habit, and things moved by nature and soul: not as such ever moved thus, but like things held by habit alone. For stones and wood, cut from the mine or having lost the growing, held by habit alone, have their mover from outside; and animals' bodies too, and portable plants, when shifted by something — not as animals and plants, but like stones and wood that lost growing. And though even these move, since all wasting bodies are in flux, their movement in wasting is consequential. Second beyond these are things moved by indwelling nature or soul — which are said to be moved from themselves by those who use names strictly. Third is the movement in animals, called movement from themselves. And the movement of rationals, I think, is movement through themselves. Remove self-movement from an animal and it can no longer be conceived as still an animal, but will be like a plant moved by nature alone or a stone carried from outside. And if something follows upon its own movement — since we named this 'being moved from itself' (Galatians 1:15) — it must be rational.

Those who want nothing to be up to us will necessarily admit most absurd things: first, that we are not animals; second, that we are not even rational — but as though moved by an outside mover, ourselves in no way moving, we are said by it to do what we are thought to do. Besides, let anyone attend to his own affections and see whether he will shamelessly say: it is not I who will, not I who eat, not I who walk, not I who assent and accept whatever doctrines, not I who nod toward others away from false ones. As it is impossible for a man to be disposed toward certain doctrines, though he invent myriad times with plausible arguments, so it is impossible to be disposed about human affairs as if the 'up to us' were in no way preserved. For who is disposed that nothing is graspable, or so lives as suspending judgment on everything whatsoever? Who does not rebuke his servant, having taken an impression of the servant's fault? Who does not accuse a son who fails his duty to parents, or blame and censure one who did shameful things, or the adulterous wife? For truth forces and compels, even though one invent myriad times, to rouse(?) and praise and blame — with the 'up to us' preserved, and what depends on us becoming praiseworthy or blameworthy.

If then the 'up to us' is preserved — having countless turnings toward virtue or vice, and again toward duty or against duty — necessarily this too, with the rest, before it happens, is known to God from creation and the world's foundation, of what sort it shall be. And in all things God predetermines, following what he has seen concerning each work of the 'up to us,' predetermining worthily for each 'up to us' movement what shall meet it from providence — and further, what shall come to pass in the sequence of future things. God's foreknowledge does not become the cause of all future things, even those to be effected from the 'up to us' according to our impulse. For even if, hypothetically, God did not know the future, we would not for that reason lose acting these things and willing those; rather, from foreknowledge comes this: that each one's 'up to us' takes order into the whole's administration, needful for the world's constitution.

If then each 'up to us' is known to him, and for this reason, as foreseen by him, providence dispenses worthily to each — it is reasonable also that what one prays, and with what disposition so-and-so believing thus and wanting this to happen to him, is grasped beforehand. before: Luke, I take it, through the 'bring us not into temptation,' (Matthew 6:13) taught in effect the 'deliver us from evil' (Psalm 4:2) too. (2 Corinthians 4:8) For by the co-working and presence of the comforting Word of God who saves us, the cheerful and undaunted state of our mind in the season of circumstances, made by God, was called enlargement.

Likewise, then, must being delivered from the evil one be conceived ... before: Not only the High Priest co-prays with the genuine prayers, but also the angels rejoicing in heaven — over one sinner repenting or over ninety-nine righteous needing no repentance — and the souls of the departed saints. This is shown when Raphael offers rational worship to God for Tobit and Sarah (for after both prayed: 'Heard,' says Scripture, 'was the prayer of both before the glory of the great Raphael, and he was sent to heal the two.' (Tobit 12:12) And Jeremiah — appearing in Maccabees, eminent in gray hair and glory, so that his eminence was something marvelous and most magnificent, holding out his right hand and giving Judas a golden sword — another departed saint bore witness, saying: 'This is he who prays much for the people and the holy city, Jeremiah, God's prophet.'

It would be absurd — with knowledge now manifest to the worthy through a mirror, in an enigma, but then revealed face to face — not to conceive the analogy for the remaining virtues, perfected then properly in those prepared in this life. One chiefest virtue by the divine word is love of neighbor — which we must conceive present far more in departed saints toward life's strugglers than among those in human weakness co-struggling with inferiors: not only here, where 'if one member suffers, all members suffer with it; if one member is glorified, all members rejoice with it' (Tobit 12:15) holds among brother-lovers. Fitting too for love beyond this life to say: 'The care of all the churches. Who is weak, and I am not weak? Who is stumbled, and I do not burn?' (2 Maccabees 15:12–16) And this, with Christ confessing that like each ailing saint he likewise ails, is in prison, goes naked and abroad, hungers and thirsts. Who reading the Gospel does not know Christ reckoning what befalls believers, by reference to himself, as his own sufferings?

If God's angels came to Jesus and ministered to him — and it is not fitting to conceive the angels' ministry to Jesus as lasting a short time of his bodily sojourn among men, with him still amid believers not as reclining but as ministering — how many angels, likely, minister to Jesus, who wants to gather Jerusalem's children one by one(?) and collect the diaspora, saving God-fearers and callers, co-working the church's growth and multitude more than the apostles: as some angels presiding over churches are named by John in Revelation? For not in vain do God's angels ascend and descend upon the Son of Man, seen by eyes lit with gnosis's light.

At prayer-time itself, then, reminded by the pray-er of what he needs, they do what they can, having received it as universal command. before: 'Thy kingdom come.' The 'kingdom of God,' according to the word of our Lord and Savior, 'comes not with observation,' 'nor shall they say: Lo here, or lo there' (Luke 17:20–21) — but 'the kingdom of God is within' us ('for the word is very nigh, in our mouth and in our heart' (Deuteronomy 30:14)). So it is plain that the one who prays for God's kingdom to come rightly prays concerning God's kingdom in himself — that it rise and bear fruit and be perfected. For every saint is ruled by God and obeys God's spiritual laws, dwelling in himself as in a well-ordered city — with the Father present to him, and Christ co-reigning with the Father in the perfected soul, according to the saying I recalled not long ago: 'We will come to him and make our abode with him.' (John 14:23) And I suppose God's kingdom is recognized as the blessed state of the ruling faculty and the ordered rank of wise reasonings, and Christ's kingdom as the progressive words, saving to their hearers, and the works of righteousness performed, and of the other virtues — for the Son of God is Word and Righteousness. But every sinner is tyrannized by the 'ruler of this age,' since every sinner is owned by the present evil age, not offering himself to him who 'gave himself for our sins, that he might deliver us from the present evil age' (Galatians 1:4) — and he 'delivers' 'according to the will of our God and Father,' (Romans 6:12) according to what is said in Galatians. And he who is tyrannized by this ruler of the age is ruled by sin by the voluntariness of his sinning. That is why Paul orders us no longer to submit when sin wills to rule us, commanding through these words: 'Let not sin, then, reign in your mortal body, to obey its lusts.' (Romans 6:12; 13:9–12)

But someone will say, to both — both the 'Hallowed be thy name' and the 'Thy kingdom come' — that if the pray-er prays to be heard, and is heard at some point, then plainly at some point God's 'name' shall be hallowed for someone, as aforesaid, and God's 'kingdom' shall stand in him. And if these things shall be his, how will he still becomingly pray concerning things present as though not present, saying 'Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come' (Philippians 3:13)? And if so, will there ever be a time when it is not becoming to say 'Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come' (1 Corinthians 15:24–28, 50–55)? We must say to this that, as one who prays to obtain a 'word of knowledge' and a 'word of wisdom' becomingly prays concerning these things always — always receiving, as he is heard, more contemplations of 'wisdom' and 'knowledge,' yet knowing 'in part' whatever at present he can hold, with the perfect, which annuls 'the partial,' 'then' to be revealed, when mind without sense assails the realities 'face to face' — so the perfect, both of hallowing God's 'name' in each of us and of his kingdom standing in him, cannot be unless the perfect 'come' also concerning 'knowledge' and 'wisdom' — and perhaps concerning the other virtues too. We journey toward perfection if we 'press toward the things before, forgetting the things behind.' (Philippians 3:13) To God's kingdom in us, then, the summit shall stand as we advance without ceasing — when what the Apostle said is fulfilled: that Christ, when all enemies are subjected to him, 'shall deliver the kingdom to God the Father, that God may be all in all.' (1 Corinthians 15:24) That is why, praying 'without ceasing,' with a disposition made godlike by the Word, we say to our Father in the heavens: 'Hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come.' (Galatians 5:22)

But concerning God's kingdom this too must be examined: that as there is no 'partnership of righteousness with lawlessness,' (2 Corinthians 6:14) nor 'fellowship of light with darkness,' nor 'concord of Christ with Beliar' — so the kingdom of sin cannot co-exist with God's kingdom. If, then, we wish to be ruled by God, let 'sin in no way reign in our mortal body,' (Romans 6:12) nor let us obey its commands, when it calls our soul to 'the works of the flesh' and things foreign to God. But 'mortifying our members on earth,' let us bear the fruits 'of the Spirit,' that as in a spiritual 'paradise' the Lord may walk in us, ruling us alone with his Christ — seated 'at his right hand' in us, from whom we pray to receive spiritual 'power' — and seated, 'until' all his enemies in us become 'the footstool of his feet,' and every principality and authority and power be annulled from us. For these things can come to be in each of us, and the last enemy be annulled — death — so that in us too it be said by Christ: 'O death, where is thy sting? O Hades, where is thy victory?' (1 Corinthians 15:24–28) Now, then, let our 'corruptible put on' holiness in continence and all purity, and 'incorruption' — and our 'mortal' be clothed, death being annulled, with the Father's 'incorruption' — so that, ruled by God, we may already be in the goods of regeneration and resurrection.

before: How a measure of confession is filled — or not filled but lacking — we may thus consider. If through the whole time of examination and trial we give no place to the devil in our hearts — who wishes to stain us with evil reasonings of denial, or double-mindedness, or any plausibility provoking toward things hostile to martyrdom and perfection — and if, besides, we stain not ourselves with any word foreign to confession, and bear all reproach and mockery and laughter and ill-fame and pity from our opponents — who deem us pitiable, supposing us deceived and foolish, calling us erring — and if we be not dragged, tugged by affection for children or their mother or any deemed dearest in life, toward possession or toward this living — but, turning from all these, become wholly God's, and of the life with him and beside him, as to share with his Only-begotten and his sharers: then may we say we filled the measure of confession. But if in even one thing we fall short, we filled it not but stained confession's measure, mixing something foreign with it. Against every virtue wars either 'the mind of the flesh,' or, more often, outward things. But for godliness alone wars the 'choice' 'race, the royal priesthood, the holy nation, the people for possession.' (1 Peter 2:9) The rest of men show, short of seeming, that — if things antagonistic to the godly exist — they purpose to die for godliness, preferring death with godliness to life with ungodliness. And each who wishes to be of the choice race is persuaded to hear God saying in every season — even when those who, on pretext of being polytheists, are atheists, plot against him — the 'Thou shalt have no other gods beside me,' (Exodus 20:3) and the 'The name of other gods you shall not remember in your hearts, nor be named from your mouth.' (Romans 10:8–10) That is why God is 'believed in the heart' by such 'unto righteousness,' and 'confessed with the mouth' by such 'unto salvation' — who grasp that neither shall they be justified unless they so believe God with their heart so disposed, nor be in salvation unless, as the disposition is, so too the word. before: When praying, then, let us not babble but theologize. We babble when, without blaming ourselves or the words of prayer we send up, we speak corrupt works or words or thoughts — lowly and blameworthy things, foreign to the Lord's incorruption. The babbler in his praying is already in a worse and harsher synagogue-condition than those named before — in a way worse than the corners in the streets — preserving not even a trace of the hypocrisy of the good. For, according to the word of the Gospel, only 'the heathen babble,' who have not even an impression of great or heavenly petitions, sending up every prayer about bodily and outward things. The one who asks lowly things of the Lord who dwells in heaven and above the heights of the heavens is likened to a babbling heathen.

And the wordy seems to babble, and the babbler to be wordy. For nothing of matter and bodies is one: each thing deemed one is split and hewn apart and divided into many, having lost unity. For the good is one, but base things are many; and truth is one, but falsehoods are many; and true righteousness is one, but many are the conditions that play the hypocrite toward it; and the wisdom of God is one, but many are the wisdoms 'of this age' and 'of the rulers of this age' (Matthew 6:7) that are being brought to nought; and the Word of God is one, but many are the words foreign to God. That is why no one shall escape 'sin' 'from wordiness,' and no one who thinks to be heard 'from wordiness' can be heard. So our prayers must not be likened to heathen who babble or are wordy or do whatever they do 'after the likeness of the serpent.' (1 Corinthians 2:6) For the God of the saints 'knows' 'before' what things his sons 'have need of,' since they are worthy of the Father's knowledge. But if anyone does not know God, he does not know the things of God either — and he does not know 'what need' he has: for the things he thinks he needs are wide of the mark. But he who has contemplated what better and more divine things he lacks, known by God, shall obtain what he contemplated, known to the Father even before the asking. So much, then, for what is said before the prayer in Matthew; now let us contemplate also what is declared by the prayer (Proverbs 10:19) (Matthew 6:8).

before: It seemed to me not unreasonable first to distinguish what is signified in Scripture, since εὐχή signifies two things — and likewise προσευχή. For this name, besides its common and customary use in many places, is also placed for what we customarily mean by εὐχή, as in the Hannah passages in First Kingdoms: And Eli the priest sat on a throne at the doorposts of the temple of the Lord. And she, bitter in soul, prayed to the Lord and wept weeping. And she vowed a vow and said: O Lord of hosts, if in oversight You look upon Your servant's humiliation and remember me and do not forget Your servant, and give Your servant a male seed — I will give him to the Lord as a gift all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head.

One might not unreasonably say here, attending to 'she prayed to the Lord' (Leviticus 27:1–8) and 'she vowed a vow': if she did both — that is, she prayed to the Lord and she vowed a vow — perhaps 'she prayed' is placed for what we customarily call prayer, while 'she vowed a vow' is placed for what is signified as ordered in Leviticus and Numbers. For 'I will give him to the Lord as a gift all the days of his life, and no razor shall come upon his head' (1 Samuel 1:9–11) is not strictly prayer but that vow — like Jephthah's in these words: And Jephthah vowed a vow to the Lord and said: If You deliver the Ammonites into my hand, then whoever comes out of my house's doors to meet me when I return in peace from the Ammonites shall be the Lord's, and I will offer him as a burnt offering (Judges 11:30–31).

before: What Jesus said, then, settling the people on the holy land, Scripture might now say to us. The wording runs: 'Now fear the Lord, and serve him in uprightness and righteousness.' (Joshua 24:14–18) And to us, persuaded to commit idolatry, it will say this and what follows, running thus: 'Put away the strange gods your fathers served beyond the river and in Egypt, and serve the Lord.' (1 Samuel 2:25) At the beginning, when you were about to be catechized, it would rightly have been said to you: 'But if it please you not to serve the Lord, choose for yourselves this day whom you shall serve — whether the gods of your fathers beyond the river, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell.' And your catechist would have said to you, 'But I and my house shall serve the Lord, for he is holy.' Now these have no place being said to you. For then you said, 'Far be it from us to forsake the Lord to serve other gods. The Lord our God himself is God, who brought us and our fathers up from Egypt, and kept us in all the way we walked in.' But in the godliness compacts too, you answered your catechists of old with this: 'We too shall serve the Lord; for this is our God.' If, then, he who transgresses compacts with men is a truce-breaker, foreign to salvation — what of those who, by denying, annul the compacts they made with God, running back to Satan, whom at baptism they renounced? To such must be said the words Eli spoke to his sons: 'If a man sinning sin against a man, they shall pray for him; but if he sin against the Lord, who shall pray for him?'

before: It is no wonder that, just as not the same shadow is given to all who receive, so to speak, the bodies that make such shadows — to some no shadow at all, to others the same shadow — so too with the prior gifts. For this is plainly seen to hold for bodies as well by those who study gnomonic problems and the ratio of shadows to the illuminating body: for gnomons are shadowless at certain seasons, and others have, so to speak, short shadows, and others longer shadows than others. It is no great thing, then, if — since the purpose of the giver who grants the prior gifts fits them by certain ineffable and mystical analogies to the receivers and to the times when the prior gifts are given — at one time no shadows at all follow the receivers, at another not all but few, at another lesser ones by comparison, with greater ones following others. As, then, one who seeks the sun's rays is neither gladdened nor grieved by the presence or absence of the bodies' shadow, having the most necessary thing — whether enlightened or deprived of the shadow, or having more or less of the shadow — so, if the spiritual gifts are with us and we are enlightened by God toward the complete possession of the true goods, we shall not fuss over a cheap matter of shadow. For all material and bodily things, whatever they may be, have the worth of a faint and feeble shadow, wholly unable to be compared with the saving and holy gifts of the God of all. For what comparison is there of bodily wealth with the wealth 'in all speech' and 'all' wisdom?

And who but a madman would compare health of flesh and bones with a healthy and vigorous soul and well-measured reasonings? All of which, ordered by the word of God, make bodily sufferings some cheap scratch — even if we count the scratch briefer than it is. But he who has contemplated what the beauty of the bride is, whose 'songs' the word of God loves — a soul in bloom with supercelestial and supermundane beauty — will be ashamed to honor with the same name of beauty the bodily beauty of woman or boy or ... Flesh is as grass, and its 'glory,' which appears in what is called the beauty of women and children, has been likened by the prophetic word to a flower, saying: 'All flesh is as grass, and all its glory as the flower of grass. The grass is withered, and the flower fallen; but the word of the Lord abides forever.' (1 Peter 1:25) But who will properly call nobility the trite thing called so among men, who has conceived the nobility of sons of God? And the mind that has contemplated Christ's 'unshakable' kingdom — how will it not despise as worth nothing 'all the kingdom upon earth' (Isaiah 40:6–8)? And having seen, as far as a human mind still bound in body can hold, and grasped as far as possible, the army of angels and archistrategi — among them powers of the Lord, archangels and thrones and dominions and principalities and authorities, supercelestial — how will it not, even if feebler than a shadow, despise as dimmest, comparing them, even these things admired among the senseless as worth no account, even if all these are given — and overlook them all, for the sake of not missing the true principalities and the more divine authorities? We must pray, then, pray concerning the prior and truly great and heavenly things, and leave the matters of the shadows that follow the prior things to God, who knows 'what need' we have, through the mortal body, 'before' we ask him (Hebrews 12:28) (Colossians 1:16 (thrones) (Matthew 6:8) (Colossians 1:16).

before: But it is likely, most God-fearing and industrious Ambrose, and most modest and courageous Tatiana — from whom, I pray, womanly frailty has already departed, as it had departed from Sarah — that you wonder why, when our treatise concerns prayer, these opening remarks have been about things impossible for men but made possible by God's grace. What I am persuaded of is this: that to expound the whole subject of prayer exactly and worthily of God — both how one must pray, and what to say to God in prayer, and which times are fitter than other times for prayer — is, given our weakness, one of those impossibilities. [Here T has illegible letters, probably a further elaboration.]

The one of these, then — I mean the 'what' — is the words of prayer; the 'how' is the disposition of the one who prays. For example, of the 'what': Ask for the great things, and the small shall be added to you; and ask for the heavenly things, and the earthly shall be added to you; and pray for those who persecute you; and beg the Lord of the harvest, therefore, to send out workers into his harvest; and pray that you may not enter into temptation. Of the 'how': pray that your flight may not be in winter or on a Sabbath; and in praying, do not babble; and whatever resembles these. Of the 'how' again: I desire then that men pray in every place, lifting holy hands without anger and doubting; and likewise that women adorn themselves in modest dress, with shame and self-control, not with braids or gold or pearls or costly clothing, but — as befits women professing godliness — with good works. Instructive of the 'how' is also this: if you bring your gift to the altar, and there remember that your brother has something against you, leave your gift there before the altar, and go first be reconciled to your brother, and then come offer your gift. For what greater gift can be sent up to God from a rational being than the fragrant word of prayer, offered from a conscience bearing no stench of sin? Further of the 'how': do not deprive one another, except by agreement for a time, that you may devote yourselves to prayer, and come together again, lest Satan test you for your lack of self-control. For the 'how' is hindered by these things, unless even the act of the marriage mysteries — things fit to be passed over in silence — becomes more solemn and slower and more passionless, when the harmony named here dissolves passion's dissonance and consumes intemperance and checks Satan's malicious gloating. Besides, instructive of the 'how' is this: whenever you stand praying, forgive whatever you hold against anyone. And Paul's word: every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head; but every woman praying or prophesying with her head unveiled dishonors her own head. You illustrate the 'how.'

But Paul knew all these things, and many times more from the Law and the prophets and the fullness of the Gospel, which he could set forth with varied exposition of each — and he speaks from a disposition not merely moderate but truthful. Yet seeing, beyond all this, how far short we fall of knowing what to pray as we ought — but what to pray as we ought, we do not know — he adds to his treatise the source from which the lack is filled: for the one who does not know, yet has made himself worthy to have the lack filled in him. For he says that the Spirit itself intercedes with unutterable groanings; and he who searches hearts knows what the mind of the Spirit is, for he intercedes for saints according to God. And the Spirit crying Abba, Father in the hearts of the blessed, which knows well the groans in the tent — groans [obscure clause, see note] the fallen and transgressors — intercedes with God with unutterable groanings, taking up our groans in great love for man and sympathy. And seeing in its wisdom our soul humbled to dust and confined in the body of humiliation, it intercedes with God not with just any groans but with certain unutterable ones, akin to the unspeakable words which no man may utter. This Spirit, then, not content with that for which it intercedes with God, straining its intercession on our behalf — concerning, I think, the more-than-conquerors, like the one who says, In all these things we are more than conquerors. And it is likely that it intercedes only for those not so great as to be more than conquerors, nor again such as to be conquered, but for conquerors.

Next, attached to 'but what to pray as we ought, we do not know, but the Spirit intercedes with unutterable groanings' (Romans 8:26) is 'I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also.' (1 Corinthians 14:15) For our mind cannot pray unless the Spirit first prays, as in accompaniment of it — just as it cannot sing and hymn the Father in Christ rhythmically, melodiously, metrically, harmoniously, unless the Spirit who searches all things, even the depths of God, first praises and hymns him whose depths it has searched and, as far as it could, grasped.

But I think some one of Jesus' disciples, sensing human weakness — falling short of how one ought to pray — and realizing this especially when he heard learned and great discourses uttered by the Savior in his prayer to the Father, said to the Lord when he stopped praying: Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples. The whole sequence of the saying runs thus: And it came to pass, as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, one of his disciples said to him: Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples to pray. For would a man reared on the Law's catechism, hearing the prophetic readings, never missing the synagogues, not have known how to pray at all until he saw the Lord praying in a certain place? To say so is absurd. He prayed according to Jewish custom, of course — but he saw that he needed a greater knowledge for prayer's ground. And what did John teach his disciples about prayer — they who came to be baptized by him from Jerusalem and all Judea and the countryside — if he did not see something more than a prophet concerning prayer, which [here T has a gap of about two lines, perhaps holding Matthew 3:5-6] it is likely he delivered not to all the baptized but in secret to those being discipled toward baptism? Such prayers, truly spiritual — the Spirit praying in the saints' hearts — were written down, full of secret and marvelous doctrines. In First Kingdoms, Hannah's prayer is partly recorded — for the whole of it, when she multiplied praying before the Lord, speaking in her heart, was not written down — and among the Psalms the sixteenth is entitled A prayer of David, and the eighty-ninth A prayer of Moses, the man of God, and the hundred and first A prayer of the afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his petition before the Lord. These prayers, since they truly were prayers, spoken in the Spirit and full of the doctrines of God's wisdom — one might say of the promises in them: Who is wise and will understand these things? And discerning, and will know them?

Since, then, expounding prayer is so great a task that we need the Father who also illuminates for this, and the firstborn Word himself teaching, and the Spirit empowering, to conceive and speak worthily of so great a proposal — having prayed as a man (for I hardly grant myself to contain prayer), I ask to obtain, before the treatise, the Spirit's prayer: that a most full and spiritual discourse may be granted us, and the prayers recorded in the Gospels clarified. Besides, instructive of the 'how' is this: whenever you stand praying, forgive whatever you hold against anyone. And Paul's word: every man praying or prophesying with his head covered dishonors his head; but every woman praying or prophesying with her head unveiled dishonors her own head. You illustrate the 'how.'

But Paul knew all these things, and many times more from the Law and the prophets and the fullness of the Gospel, which he could set forth with varied exposition of each — and he speaks from a disposition not merely moderate but truthful. Yet seeing, beyond all this, how far short we fall of knowing what to pray as we ought — but what to pray as we ought, we do not know — he adds to his treatise the source from which the lack is filled: for the one who does not know, yet has made himself worthy to have the lack filled in him. For he says that the Spirit itself intercedes with unutterable groanings; and he who searches hearts knows what the mind of the Spirit is, for he intercedes for saints according to God. And the Spirit crying Abba, Father in the hearts of the blessed, which knows well the groans in the tent — groans [obscure clause, see note] the fallen and transgressors — intercedes with God with unutterable groanings, taking up our groans in great love for man and sympathy. And seeing in its wisdom our soul humbled to dust and confined in the body of humiliation, it intercedes with God not with just any groans but with certain unutterable ones, akin to the unspeakable words which no man may utter. This Spirit, then, not content with that for which it intercedes with God, straining its intercession on our behalf — concerning, I think, the more-than-conquerors, like the one who says, In all these things we are more than conquerors. And it is likely that it intercedes only for those not so great as to be more than conquerors, nor again such as to be conquered, but for conquerors.

Next, attached to 'but what to pray as we ought, we do not know, but the Spirit intercedes with unutterable groanings' (Romans 8:26) is 'I will pray with the spirit, and I will pray with the mind also; I will sing with the spirit, and I will sing with the mind also.' (1 Corinthians 14:15) For our mind cannot pray unless the Spirit first prays, as in accompaniment of it — just as it cannot sing and hymn the Father in Christ rhythmically, melodiously, metrically, harmoniously, unless the Spirit who searches all things, even the depths of God, first praises and hymns him whose depths it has searched and, as far as it could, grasped.

But I think some one of Jesus' disciples, sensing human weakness — falling short of how one ought to pray — and realizing this especially when he heard learned and great discourses uttered by the Savior in his prayer to the Father, said to the Lord when he stopped praying: Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples. The whole sequence of the saying runs thus: And it came to pass, as he was praying in a certain place, when he ceased, one of his disciples said to him: Lord, teach us to pray, as John also taught his disciples to pray. For would a man reared on the Law's catechism, hearing the prophetic readings, never missing the synagogues, not have known how to pray at all until he saw the Lord praying in a certain place? To say so is absurd. He prayed according to Jewish custom, of course — but he saw that he needed a greater knowledge for prayer's ground. And what did John teach his disciples about prayer — they who came to be baptized by him from Jerusalem and all Judea and the countryside — if he did not see something more than a prophet concerning prayer, which [here T has a gap of about two lines, perhaps holding Matthew 3:5-6] it is likely he delivered not to all the baptized but in secret to those being discipled toward baptism? Such prayers, truly spiritual — the Spirit praying in the saints' hearts — were written down, full of secret and marvelous doctrines. In First Kingdoms, Hannah's prayer is partly recorded — for the whole of it, when she multiplied praying before the Lord, speaking in her heart, was not written down — and among the Psalms the sixteenth is entitled A prayer of David, and the eighty-ninth A prayer of Moses, the man of God, and the hundred and first A prayer of the afflicted, when he is faint and pours out his petition before the Lord. These prayers, since they truly were prayers, spoken in the Spirit and full of the doctrines of God's wisdom — one might say of the promises in them: Who is wise and will understand these things? And discerning, and will know them?

Since, then, expounding prayer is so great a task that we need the Father who also illuminates for this, and the firstborn Word himself teaching, and the Spirit empowering, to conceive and speak worthily of so great a proposal — having prayed as a man (for I hardly grant myself to contain prayer), I ask to obtain, before the treatise, the Spirit's prayer: that a most full and spiritual discourse may be granted us, and the prayers recorded in the Gospels clarified. And first of all it must be observed that Matthew and Luke might seem to most to have recorded the same prayer outlined for how we must pray. But the words of Matthew run in this way: 'Our Father who art in the heavens, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; thy will be done, as in heaven, also upon earth; give us this day our daily bread; and forgive us our debts, as we also have forgiven our debtors; and bring us not into temptation, but deliver us from evil.' (Matthew 6:9–13) And those of Luke: 'Father, hallowed be thy name; thy kingdom come; our daily bread give us day by day; and forgive us our sins, for we ourselves also forgive everyone indebted to us; and bring us not into temptation.' (Luke 11:2–4)

But we must say to those who suppose so, first, that the phrases, though neighboring one another in some things, are plainly seen to differ in others, as we shall show when we examine them; and second, that it is impossible for the same prayer to have been spoken both on the mountain — where, seeing the crowds, he went up, and when he had sat down his disciples came to him, and opening his mouth he taught (for it stands recorded with Matthew in the sequence of the announcement concerning the beatitudes and the commandments that follow) — and 'when he was in a certain place' (Matthew 5:1–2) praying, 'when he ceased,' spoken to one of the disciples who asked to be taught — presumably not present then, when he spoke the words in Matthew, or not retaining what had long ago been said. Or perhaps it is better to consider the prayers different, having some parts in common. And though we searched Mark as well, lest any equivalent recorded prayer escape us, we found not even a trace of a prayer lying there (Luke 11:1).
